46960.q: In which Swiss region is Kim Jong-un said by media reports to have gone to school in the 1990s?
46960.e: According to reports, he attended schools in Gümligen and Liebefeld near Bern under a false name. This is not completely certain, but the authorities confirmed a North Korean pupil in Köniz.
46960.m: Kim Jong-un is said to have gone to school near Bern as a teenager.

46961.q: Which half-brother of Kim Jong-un was killed with a nerve agent at Kuala Lumpur airport in 2017?
46961.e: Kim Jong-nam was attacked with the nerve agent VX in February 2017 and died shortly afterwards. He was Kim Jong-il's eldest son and lived in exile.
46961.m: Kim Jong-nam was murdered with VX in Malaysia in 2017.

46962.q: Which party has governed North Korea since the state was founded?
46962.e: The Workers' Party of Korea is the leading state party; other permitted parties are subordinate to it. Kim Jong-un has been at its head since 2012.
46962.m: North Korea is dominated by the Workers' Party of Korea.

46963.q: According to current research, where was Kim Jong-il actually born?
46963.e: Official propaganda names a secret camp on the sacred Mount Paektu. Historians, however, believe he was born in 1941 in a Soviet military camp near Khabarovsk.
46963.m: Kim Jong-il's birth on Mount Paektu is a propaganda legend.

46964.q: What is the central idea of North Korea's Juche ideology?
46964.e: Juche is usually translated as “self-reliance” or “independence”. The country should not depend on others politically, economically or militarily.
46964.m: Juche stands for the idea of national self-reliance.

46965.q: With which year does North Korea's Juche calendar begin?
46965.e: Juche year 1 is 1912, the year Kim Il-sung was born. The calendar was introduced in 1997.
46965.m: The Juche calendar begins with Kim Il-sung's birth year, 1912.

46966.q: What does the Juche Tower in Pyongyang stand for?
a: The state ideology and Kim Il-sung
46966.e: The 170-metre tower was opened in 1982 for Kim Il-sung's 70th birthday. It is said to consist of 25,550 granite blocks, one for each day of Kim Il-sung's life up to then.
46966.m: The Juche Tower honours the state ideology and Kim Il-sung.

46967.q: According to official teaching, which three principles form the core of Juche?
46967.e: The principles are called chaju (political independence), charip (economic self-sufficiency) and chawi (military self-defence). They are meant to make the country independent of foreign powers.
46967.m: Juche demands political, economic and military independence.

46968.q: Who is officially regarded in North Korea as the founder of the Juche ideology?
46968.e: North Korean propaganda credits Juche to Kim Il-sung. The doctrine was largely worked out by the philosopher Hwang Jang-yop, who fled to South Korea in 1997.
46968.m: In North Korea, Juche is regarded as Kim Il-sung's teaching.

46969.q: Which ideology was gradually pushed out of the North Korean constitution by Juche?
46969.e: Juche was written into the constitution as the guiding ideology in 1972 and gradually displaced Marxism-Leninism. In 2009 the word “communism” disappeared from the constitution.
46969.m: In North Korea, Juche replaced Marxism-Leninism as the state ideology.

46970.q: What is North Korea's official state ideology, which extends Juche with the teachings of the leaders, often called today as a whole?
46970.e: Since 2012 the party has spoken of Kimilsungism-Kimjongilism. This declares the teachings of the two dead leaders to be the binding foundation.
46970.m: North Korea's state ideology is called Kimilsungism-Kimjongilism.

46971.q: What consequence of the goal of economic self-sufficiency became especially clear after the collapse of the Soviet Union?
46971.e: Without Soviet aid and because of failed harvests, a famine known as the “Arduous March” struck in the mid-1990s. Estimates suggest hundreds of thousands died.
46971.m: Isolation contributed to a famine in North Korea in the 1990s.

46972.q: What reason did the army give for the 2021 coup in Myanmar?
46972.e: The military claimed fraud in the November 2020 election, which the NLD had clearly won. The election commission and observers found no evidence of it.
46972.m: The army justified the coup with alleged electoral fraud.

46973.q: Which sign did demonstrators in Myanmar use in 2021 as a symbol of resistance?
46973.e: The three-finger salute comes from “The Hunger Games” films. It had already been used at protests in Thailand.
46973.m: The three-finger salute became the sign of protest in Myanmar.

46974.q: What is the opposition government formed by removed members of parliament in Myanmar called?
46974.e: The National Unity Government (NUG) was formed in April 2021. It sees itself as the legitimate government and works underground and in exile.
46974.m: The National Unity Government is the opposition government to Myanmar's junta.

46975.q: Who took over the leadership of Myanmar after the coup of 1 February 2021?
a: An administrator appointed by the UN
46975.e: Commander-in-chief Min Aung Hlaing put himself at the head of the junta, which ruled through a so-called State Administration Council. The elected head of government, Aung San Suu Kyi, was arrested.
46975.m: After the 2021 coup, army chief Min Aung Hlaing ruled.

46976.q: What was the movement called in which doctors, teachers and civil servants stopped work after the coup?
46976.e: In the Civil Disobedience Movement many state employees refused to work for the junta. Medical staff led the way.
46976.m: After the coup many state employees stopped work in civil disobedience.

46977.q: Roughly how long did the military rule Myanmar (Burma) after the first coup in 1962, until the country partly opened up from 2011?
46977.e: General Ne Win staged a coup on 2 March 1962. After that the military ruled in various forms for almost five decades.
46977.m: In Myanmar the military ruled long before the 2021 coup.

46978.q: Why was Aung San Suu Kyi not allowed to become president of Myanmar under the 2008 constitution?
a: She was too old for the office.
She had never been a member of parliament.
Women were excluded from the office.
46978.e: The constitution excludes people whose spouse or children are citizens of another country. Her sons are British, so in 2016 the office of State Counsellor was created for her.
46978.m: Because of her British sons, Aung San Suu Kyi could not become president.

46979.q: Before which court did Aung San Suu Kyi defend Myanmar in 2019 against the accusation of genocide against the Rohingya?
46979.e: The Gambia had brought a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in The Hague. Her appearance there badly damaged her international reputation.
46979.m: In 2019 Aung San Suu Kyi defended Myanmar in The Hague against the genocide accusation.

46980.q: What did the military in Myanmar do with Aung San Suu Kyi after the coup in February 2021?
a: It had her arrested and convicted several times
It sent her into exile in Britain
It used her as a mediator
46980.e: Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested during the coup. In a series of trials before military courts her sentences added up to 33 years; observers consider the proceedings politically motivated.
46980.m: After the coup Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested and given a long prison sentence.

46981.q: What did Ferdinand Marcos impose in 1972 in order to stay in power?
46981.e: Shortly before the end of his last permitted term, Marcos imposed martial law and ruled by decree. He formally lifted it only in 1981 but remained in power as an authoritarian ruler until 1986.
46981.m: With martial law in 1972, Marcos made himself a dictator.

46982.q: Which son of Ferdinand Marcos became president of the Philippines in 2022?
46982.e: Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. won the 2022 election clearly. The family thus returned to power 36 years after fleeing.
46982.m: Since 2022 Marcos's son Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has been president of the Philippines.

46983.q: After which road in Manila is the People Power Revolution also named?
46983.e: Hundreds of thousands gathered on Epifanio de los Santos Avenue, EDSA for short, in February 1986. That is why the uprising is also called the EDSA Revolution.
46983.m: The People Power Revolution is also known as the EDSA Revolution.

46984.q: What began in Indonesia after Suharto resigned in 1998?
46984.e: Vice-President B. J. Habibie took over the office. Under him the democratisation known as “Reformasi” began, with free elections in 1999.
46984.m: After Suharto, Indonesia's path to democracy began in 1998.

46985.q: What role did the army have in Indonesia under Suharto?
a: Besides defence, it also had political power
It was completely excluded from politics
It was under the command of the United Nations
It consisted only of foreign mercenaries
46985.e: The principle of “Dwifungsi” (dual function) gave the military a role in politics and administration as well as defence. Officers held seats in parliament and posts in ministries.
46985.m: With Dwifungsi, Indonesia's army secured political power.

46986.q: How did Park Chung-hee come to power in South Korea in 1961?
46986.e: On 16 May 1961 a group of officers under Park overthrew the government. From 1963 he ruled as an elected president, increasingly in an authoritarian way.
46986.m: Park Chung-hee seized power in South Korea in a coup in 1961.

46987.q: What did South Korea's 1972 constitution allow President Park Chung-hee?
a: Unlimited re-election and sweeping emergency powers
46987.e: The so-called Yushin Constitution (“renewal”) made Park practically the sole ruler. It remained in force until his death in 1979.
46987.m: With the 1972 constitution Park strengthened his dictatorship.

46988.q: How did Park Chung-hee's rule end in 1979?
a: He was shot by the head of the intelligence service.
He was replaced through an election.
46988.e: On 26 October 1979 Kim Jae-gyu, director of the KCIA intelligence service, killed him at a dinner. His motives are still disputed today.
46988.m: Park Chung-hee was shot in 1979 by his own intelligence chief.

46989.q: What is South Korea's rapid economic boom under Park Chung-hee often called?
46989.e: The Han flows through Seoul. Under Park, South Korea became an industrial nation through state-directed export promotion.
46989.m: The boom under Park is called the Miracle on the Han River.

46990.q: What are the large family-run business groups that Park Chung-hee deliberately promoted called?
46990.e: Chaebol such as Samsung, Hyundai or LG received cheap loans and export advantages. Keiretsu and zaibatsu are Japanese forms.
46990.m: Park promoted South Korea's family business groups, the chaebol.

46991.q: What was the aim of the Saemaul Movement, which Park Chung-hee launched in South Korea in 1970?
a: To abolish the family business groups
46991.e: The “New Village Movement” improved roads, houses and farming. It combined development with political mobilisation.
46991.m: The Saemaul Movement was meant to modernise South Korea's villages.

46992.q: Which daughter of Park Chung-hee became president of South Korea in 2013?
46992.e: Park Geun-hye was the first woman to be president of South Korea. In 2017 she was removed from office over a corruption scandal.
46992.m: Park Chung-hee's daughter Park Geun-hye became president in 2013.

46993.q: Which intelligence service did the military government under Park Chung-hee found in 1961?
46993.e: The Korean Central Intelligence Agency watched and persecuted opponents. Its successor today is called the National Intelligence Service (NIS).
46993.m: The KCIA intelligence service was created under Park in 1961.

46994.q: From when to when was martial law in force in Taiwan?
46994.e: Martial law came into force on 20 May 1949 and was lifted on 15 July 1987. At 38 years, it was one of the longest in the world.
46994.m: Taiwan was under martial law for 38 years, from 1949 to 1987.

46995.q: What is the period of political persecution in Taiwan under martial law called?
46995.e: During the “White Terror”, tens of thousands were arrested as supposed communists or separatists. Thousands were executed.
46995.m: The persecution under Taiwan's martial law is called the White Terror.

46996.q: Which event of 1947 is seen as the start of violent repression in Taiwan?
46996.e: After a dispute over illegal cigarettes an uprising broke out, which the Kuomintang crushed bloodily. Thousands of people were killed; 28 February is now a day of remembrance.
46996.m: The 28 February Incident of 1947 is a trauma for Taiwan.

46997.q: Which party ruled Taiwan alone during martial law?
46997.e: The Kuomintang (Nationalist Party) had fled to Taiwan under Chiang Kai-shek. New parties were banned during martial law.
46997.m: Under martial law the Kuomintang ruled Taiwan alone.

46998.q: Who lifted martial law in Taiwan in 1987?
46998.e: Chiang Ching-kuo, son of Chiang Kai-shek, started the opening up towards the end of his life. He died in 1988.
46998.m: Chiang Ching-kuo ended martial law in Taiwan in 1987.

46999.q: Which opposition party was founded in Taiwan in 1986, although new parties were still banned?
46999.e: The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) was proclaimed on 28 September 1986. The government tolerated it, a sign that liberalisation was beginning.
46999.m: The DPP was founded in 1986, while martial law was still in force.

47000.q: How did Taiwan develop after martial law ended in 1987?
a: It became a democracy with free elections
It became part of the People's Republic of China
It was ruled by the army
47000.e: After martial law ended, parties and the press became free. In 1996 Taiwan elected its president directly for the first time, and in 2000 the opposition DPP won for the first time.
47000.m: After martial law, Taiwan became a democracy.

47001.q: On which island was Taiwan's best-known prison for political prisoners?
47001.e: Thousands of political prisoners were held on Green Island off the east coast. Today a human rights museum there remembers them.
47001.m: Many of Taiwan's political prisoners were held on Green Island.

47002.q: In which year did the Khmer Rouge capture the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh?
47002.e: On 17 April 1975 the Khmer Rouge marched into Phnom Penh. In 1979 they were overthrown by Vietnam.
47002.m: The Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh in 1975.

47003.q: Roughly how many people died under Khmer Rouge rule?
47003.e: Executions, forced labour, hunger and disease killed about a quarter of the population. Most estimates are between 1.5 and 2 million dead.
47003.m: Under the Khmer Rouge about a quarter of Cambodians died.

47004.q: What was the name of the S-21 torture prison in Phnom Penh, which is now a museum?
47004.e: An estimated 20,000 people were held in the former Tuol Sleng secondary school, and almost all of them were killed. Choeung Ek, by contrast, is the nearby execution site.
47004.m: The S-21 prison was called Tuol Sleng.

47005.q: What did the Khmer Rouge do with the cities immediately after taking power?
a: They handed them over to Vietnam.
47005.e: The people of Phnom Penh and other cities were driven into the countryside. The aim was a classless farming society starting from “Year Zero”.
47005.m: The Khmer Rouge drove city dwellers into the countryside.

47006.q: Which country ended Khmer Rouge rule with an invasion in January 1979?
47006.e: Vietnamese troops took Phnom Penh on 7 January 1979. The Khmer Rouge retreated into the jungle on the Thai border.
47006.m: Vietnam overthrew the Khmer Rouge regime in 1979.

47007.q: What did the Khmer Rouge call their state?
47007.e: The official name was Democratic Kampuchea. The People's Republic of Kampuchea was the successor state backed by Vietnam.
47007.m: The Khmer Rouge state was called Democratic Kampuchea.

47008.q: What kind of court convicted leading Khmer Rouge members from 2010?
a: A UN-backed special tribunal in Cambodia
The International Court of Justice in The Hague
47008.e: In 2010 the Khmer Rouge Tribunal first convicted Duch, the head of S-21 prison. Later came verdicts against Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan.
47008.m: A UN-backed special tribunal convicted leading Khmer Rouge members.

47009.q: Which 1984 film made the crimes of the Khmer Rouge known around the world?
47009.e: The film tells the story of the reporter Sydney Schanberg and his Cambodian colleague Dith Pran. Its title became the term for Cambodia's mass graves.
47009.m: The film “The Killing Fields” gave Cambodia's mass graves their name.

47010.q: Which event in 1932 ended the absolute monarchy in Thailand?
47010.e: On 24 June 1932 the “People's Party” of officers and officials took power. Since then Thailand has been a constitutional monarchy.
47010.m: A coup made Thailand a constitutional monarchy in 1932.

47011.q: Which prime minister was overthrown in a military coup in 2006 while he was in New York?
47011.e: Thaksin was attending the UN General Assembly on 19 September 2006 when the army staged a coup in Bangkok. Afterwards he lived in exile for a long time.
47011.m: Thaksin Shinawatra was overthrown in a coup in 2006.

47012.q: Which general led the coup in Thailand in May 2014 and then became head of government?
47012.e: Army chief Prayut Chan-o-cha took power on 22 May 2014. He remained prime minister until 2023.
47012.m: Prayut Chan-o-cha staged a coup in 2014 and ruled Thailand until 2023.

47013.q: What did the Thai junta have drawn up after the 2014 coup to secure the military's influence in the long term?
47013.e: The junta ruled as the “National Council for Peace and Order” until 2019. Among other things, the 2017 constitution allowed the military to choose the Senate.
47013.m: After the 2014 coup, Thailand's military secured its influence with a new constitution.

47014.q: Which law in Thailand punishes insulting the royal family with long prison sentences?
47014.e: Article 112 of the criminal code provides for up to 15 years in prison per offence. After the 2014 coup it was used especially often.
47014.m: Thailand's lèse-majesté law provides for harsh penalties.

47015.q: Who intervened in Thailand in 1992, so that the coup general Suchinda resigned after bloody protests?
47015.e: During “Black May” 1992 the military fired on demonstrators in Bangkok. King Bhumibol summoned the opponents, after which Suchinda resigned.
47015.m: In 1992 pressure from the people and the king forced a coup general to resign.

47016.q: What happened in Thailand in 1976 immediately after a massacre of protesting students in Bangkok?
47016.e: On 6 October 1976 security forces and militias attacked students at Thammasat University, and dozens died. That same evening the military staged a coup.
47016.m: In 1976 the Thammasat massacre was followed by a military coup.

47017.q: Roughly how many times has Thailand had a new constitution since 1932, partly because of the many coups?
47017.e: After almost every coup the constitution was scrapped and rewritten. The current constitution dates from 2017 and is roughly the twentieth.
47017.m: Because of many coups, Thailand has had about 20 constitutions.

47018.q: Which country did Saparmurat Niyazov rule until his death in 2006?
47018.e: Niyazov already led Turkmenistan as the Soviet party chief and, from independence in 1991, as president. He died in December 2006.

47019.q: What did Niyazov have placed on a large monument in Ashgabat?
a: a golden statue that turned with the sun
a stone figure of his mother
a huge clock with his face
47019.e: The gilded statue turned so that it always faced the sun. After his death the monument was moved to the edge of the city.
47019.m: In Ashgabat a golden Niyazov statue turned with the sun.

47020.q: Which status did Niyazov have the Turkmen parliament give him in 1999?
47020.e: In 1999 parliament made him president for life. After that, no presidential elections were held until his death.
47020.m: From 1999 Niyazov was president for life.

47021.q: Which foreign policy status of Turkmenistan did the UN General Assembly recognise in 1995?
a: a seat on the Security Council
47021.e: On 12 December 1995 the UN recognised Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality. The Arch of Neutrality in Ashgabat commemorates this.
47021.m: Since 1995 Turkmenistan has been a neutral state recognised by the UN.

47022.q: What did Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov build up in Turkmenistan after 2006 as Niyazov's successor?
47022.e: The former health minister took power in 2006. He too had himself honoured with statues and handed the presidency to his son in 2022.
47022.m: Niyazov was followed by a new personality cult under Berdimuhamedov.

47023.q: When did the National Security Law come into force in Hong Kong?
47023.e: The Standing Committee of the National People's Congress in Beijing passed the law on 30 June 2020. It came into force that same evening, shortly before the anniversary of the handover.
47023.m: Hong Kong's security law has applied since 30 June 2020.

47024.q: Which four offences does Hong Kong's National Security Law punish?
a: Secession, subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign forces
Espionage, corruption, tax fraud and treason
Riot, theft, blackmail and drug dealing
High treason, perjury, espionage and sabotage
47024.e: The law names secession, subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign forces. The maximum penalty is life imprisonment.
47024.m: Hong Kong's security law targets four offences, with sentences up to life imprisonment.

47025.q: What is the group of democracy activists called who were charged over an unofficial primary election in 2020?
47025.e: The 47 defendants had organised or taken part in a primary election of the pro-democracy camp in 2020. The authorities treated this as an attempt at subversion; in 2024 prison sentences of up to ten years were handed down.
47025.m: The “Hong Kong 47” were convicted of subversion over a primary election.

47026.q: What caused a first attempt to introduce Hong Kong's own security law to fail in 2003?
a: A ruling by a UN court
47026.e: Article 23 of Hong Kong's Basic Law requires a local law against treason and subversion. After large demonstrations the draft was withdrawn in 2003; in March 2024 such a law was passed without resistance.
47026.m: In 2003 mass protests prevented a security law in Hong Kong.

47027.q: Which new authority did Beijing set up directly in Hong Kong with the security law?
a: an office for safeguarding national security
a Hong Kong People's Liberation Army
a Hong Kong ministry of state security
47027.e: The Central Government's Office for Safeguarding National Security reports directly to Beijing. It is not subject to Hong Kong's courts.
47027.m: With the law, Beijing got its own security office in Hong Kong.

47028.q: What is the mausoleum in Pyongyang called, where Kim Il-sung and Kim Jong-il lie embalmed?
47028.e: Kim Il-sung's former official residence was turned into a mausoleum after his death. Since 2012 Kim Jong-il has also lain in state there.
47028.m: The two dead Kim leaders lie in the Kumsusan Palace of the Sun.

47029.q: Which politician, winner of the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize, was arrested during the 2021 coup in Myanmar?
47029.e: Aung San Suu Kyi led the government after her party, the NLD, had clearly won the elections. In the early hours of the coup she was arrested, as was President Win Myint.
47029.m: Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested in the 2021 coup.

47030.q: For how long did the military in Myanmar initially declare a state of emergency after the coup?
47030.e: On the day of the coup the army declared a one-year emergency and promised new elections afterwards. However, the state of emergency was extended several times.
47030.m: Myanmar's state of emergency, at first for one year, was extended again and again.

47031.q: What did an alliance of rebel groups in Myanmar achieve from October 2023?
a: It captured large areas from the junta
It made peace with the army
47031.e: With “Operation 1027”, the so-called Three Brotherhood Alliance captured many military posts and border towns in northern Shan State. This put the junta under heavy military pressure.
47031.m: From October 2023 the junta in Myanmar lost large areas to rebels.

47032.q: Whose daughter is Aung San Suu Kyi?
47032.e: Her father Aung San led Burma to independence and was murdered in 1947, when she was two years old. His reputation contributed a lot to her role in the opposition.
47032.m: Aung San Suu Kyi is the daughter of the national hero Aung San.

47033.q: Why did Aung San Suu Kyi not travel to Britain in 1999 to see her terminally ill husband?
a: She feared she would not be allowed back in.
She was facing charges in London at the time.
47033.e: Her husband, the Tibet scholar Michael Aris, died of cancer in 1999. The junta refused him entry, and she stayed in the country because she feared leaving with no return.
47033.m: Aung San Suu Kyi stayed in Myanmar in 1999 so as not to be locked out.

47034.q: Which human rights prize of the European Parliament did Aung San Suu Kyi receive in 1990?
47034.e: The Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought has been awarded since 1988. She received it a year before an even more famous award from Oslo.
47034.m: Aung San Suu Kyi received the Sakharov Prize in 1990.

47035.q: What is Aung San Suu Kyi's well-known 1991 collection of essays called?
47035.e: “Freedom from Fear” contains speeches and essays on democracy and human rights. The title essay describes fear as the basis of all oppression.
47035.m: Aung San Suu Kyi's best-known book is called “Freedom from Fear”.

47036.q: How did the military junta react to the election victory of Aung San Suu Kyi's party in 1990?
a: It did not recognise the result.
It formed a coalition with her.
It had the election held again.
47036.e: The opposition won around 80 per cent of the seats, but the military did not hand over power. Many elected members of parliament were arrested or fled.
47036.m: In 1990 the junta ignored the opposition's clear election victory.

47037.q: In which year was Ferdinand Marcos first elected president of the Philippines?
47037.e: Marcos won the 1965 election and was re-elected in 1969. The constitution would not have allowed a third term.
47037.m: Ferdinand Marcos became president of the Philippines in 1965.

47038.q: Where did Ferdinand Marcos flee in 1986 after the mass protests of the People Power Revolution?
47038.e: The USA flew Marcos and his family out to Hawaii. He died there in exile in 1989 without ever returning to the Philippines.
47038.m: Ferdinand Marcos died in exile in Hawaii in 1989.

47039.q: Where was Ferdinand Marcos buried in 2016 on the orders of President Duterte?
a: in the Heroes' Cemetery in Manila
47039.e: The burial at the Libingan ng mga Bayani sparked fierce protests. Victims of the dictatorship saw it as honouring the dictator.
47039.m: Marcos's burial in the Heroes' Cemetery in 2016 was controversial.

47040.q: Which institution called on the people to protest during the 1986 People Power Revolution in the Philippines?
47040.e: Cardinal Jaime Sin used the church radio station Radio Veritas to call on people to protect the rebel soldiers. Hundreds of thousands then poured onto the streets.
47040.m: In 1986 the Catholic Church mobilised the masses against Marcos.

47041.q: Which general, later president himself, turned away from Marcos in 1986 together with Defence Minister Enrile?
47041.e: Fidel Ramos and Juan Ponce Enrile barricaded themselves with their troops in two military camps in Manila. Ramos was president from 1992 to 1998.
47041.m: Fidel Ramos went over to the rebels in 1986.

47042.q: How long did the popular uprising of the People Power Revolution last in February 1986?
47042.e: The uprising lasted from 22 to 25 February 1986. On the last day Marcos left the presidential palace.
47042.m: The People Power Revolution brought down Marcos in just four days.

47043.q: How did Suharto come to power in Indonesia from 1966?
a: President Sukarno had to hand him sweeping powers
He won a free presidential election
He was installed by the United Nations
He inherited the office from his father
47043.e: With a document dated 11 March 1966, the “Supersemar”, Suharto received special powers. He used them to ban the Communist Party and gradually pushed Sukarno out of office.
47043.m: Suharto's takeover began in 1966 with the Supersemar.

47044.q: How did Suharto secure large majorities in each election?
a: With an alliance of all opposition parties
With the votes of Indonesians abroad
With a coalition with the communists
47044.e: Golkar, an association of civil servants, soldiers and other groups, won every election under Suharto with a large majority. Other parties were heavily restricted.

47045.q: Which event did Suharto use in 1965 to take control in Indonesia?
a: An attempted coup in which six generals were murdered
A victory in a war against Australia
The sudden death of President Sukarno
An uprising against Dutch colonial rule
47045.e: On the night of 30 September to 1 October 1965 the “30 September Movement” murdered six generals. Suharto put down the coup attempt and blamed the communists, after which mass killings followed.
47045.m: An attempted coup in 1965 paved Suharto's way to power.

47046.q: What was the aim of the “Transmigrasi” programme under Suharto?
a: To resettle people from Java on other islands
To send Indonesian workers to Europe
To move the capital to another island
To expel all foreigners from Indonesia
47046.e: The programme was meant to reduce overpopulation on Java and develop remote islands. In many places it led to conflicts with the local population.
47046.m: With Transmigrasi, Indonesia resettled people from Java on other islands.

47047.q: What role did the state philosophy Pancasila have under Suharto from 1985?
a: All parties and organisations had to accept it as their sole foundation
It was banned and its followers were persecuted
It applied only to the army
It was a religious teaching for Muslims only
47047.e: Pancasila consists of five principles, including belief in God and national unity. Suharto used it to discipline political and religious opponents.
47047.m: Under Suharto, Pancasila was the compulsory state ideology.

47048.q: What does the abbreviation KKN, which the 1998 student protests against Suharto denounced, stand for?
47048.e: The protesters accused Suharto of enriching his family and friends. His children owned large parts of the economy.
47048.m: In 1998 students protested against corruption, collusion and nepotism.

47049.q: How did the Khmer Rouge leadership present itself to the population?
a: It appeared on television every day
It allowed itself to be freely elected
It ruled from exile in Paris
47049.e: The party called itself “Angkar”, which means “the Organisation”. The identity of the leadership around Pol Pot remained hidden from the population for a long time.
47049.m: The Khmer Rouge demanded obedience to an anonymous leadership.

47050.q: Which art forms did Niyazov ban as “un-Turkmen”?
47050.e: In 2001 Niyazov had the opera and ballet company dissolved. He considered these art forms foreign to Turkmen culture.
47050.m: Niyazov banned opera and ballet in Turkmenistan.

47051.q: Which office did Niyazov already hold before Turkmenistan became independent?
a: First Secretary of the Communist Party
47051.e: From 1985 he led the Communist Party of the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic. After 1991 he remained in power without a break.
47051.m: Niyazov was already Turkmenistan's party chief in Soviet times.

47052.q: Which controversial order did Niyazov give in the health service in 2005?
a: Closing the hospitals outside the capital
Building a chain of hospitals in every village
47052.e: Niyazov justified the closures by saying sick people should come to Ashgabat. Care for people in the countryside got much worse.
47052.m: In 2005 Niyazov had the hospitals outside Ashgabat closed.

47053.q: According to Article 38, to whom does Hong Kong's security law apply?
a: also to foreigners outside Hong Kong
only to residents of Hong Kong
only to people on the mainland
47053.e: Article 38 also covers acts by non-residents outside Hong Kong. Critics see this as a claim to prosecute people worldwide.
47053.m: Hong Kong's security law claims to apply worldwide.

47054.q: How did many well-known democracy activists in Hong Kong react when the security law came into force in 2020?
a: They dissolved their groups or fled abroad
47054.e: The party Demosisto of the activist Joshua Wong dissolved itself on 30 June 2020. Co-founder Nathan Law went into exile in London.
47054.m: The security law crushed the democracy movement in Hong Kong.

47055.q: Because of which protest slogan, among other things, was the first defendant under the security law convicted in 2021?
a: “Liberate Hong Kong, revolution of our times”
47055.e: Tong Ying-kit had driven into police officers carrying a flag with this slogan. The court treated the slogan as a call for secession and sentenced him to nine years in prison.
47055.m: The slogan “Liberate Hong Kong, revolution of our times” is treated as a crime.

47056.q: In which city was the White Rose resistance group mainly active?
47056.e: The White Rose consisted mainly of students at the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich. From there they spread their leaflets in 1942 and 1943.
47056.m: The White Rose was a student resistance group in Munich.

47057.q: Which subject did Hans Scholl, Alexander Schmorell and Willi Graf study?
47057.e: The three were medical students and were therefore sent to the Eastern Front as medics in 1942. Their experiences there strengthened their resistance.
47057.m: Several members of the White Rose were medical students.

47058.q: When were Hans and Sophie Scholl executed after being sentenced to death in February 1943?
a: Shortly before the end of the war in 1945
Not at all, they were pardoned
47058.e: The siblings were sentenced on 22 February 1943 and executed by guillotine a few hours later in Munich-Stadelheim prison.
47058.m: Hans and Sophie Scholl died on the day they were sentenced.

47059.q: Which court sentenced Hans Scholl, Sophie Scholl and Christoph Probst to death in February 1943?
47059.e: The People's Court under its president Roland Freisler sat specially in Munich for this. The sentence was carried out the same day, 22 February 1943.
47059.m: The People's Court was the special political court of the Nazi state.

47060.q: Which Munich professor belonged to the White Rose and wrote the sixth leaflet?
47060.e: The philosopher and musicologist Kurt Huber wrote the draft of the sixth leaflet. He too was sentenced to death and executed in 1943.
47060.m: Kurt Huber was the professor in the White Rose circle.

47061.q: How did the text of the White Rose's sixth leaflet reach Germany in large numbers after its authors had died?
a: It was read out on the radio
Churches handed it out after Mass
47061.e: The leaflet was smuggled to Britain via Scandinavia. In 1943 the Royal Air Force dropped it in large numbers over Germany.
47061.m: The Allies spread the White Rose's last leaflet from the air.

47062.q: Who did NOT belong to the inner circle of the White Rose?
47062.e: Schmorell, Graf and Probst were students in the circle around Hans Scholl. Stauffenberg was an officer who belonged to a different resistance group.
47062.m: The core of the White Rose was made up mainly of young students.

47063.q: Which member of the White Rose was born in Russia?
47063.e: Schmorell was born in Orenburg in 1917 and grew up in Munich from 1921. The Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia declared him a saint in 2012.

47064.q: Who planted the bomb in Hitler's headquarters on 20 July 1944?
47064.e: As chief of staff of the Replacement Army, Stauffenberg was invited to the briefing and brought the bomb in a briefcase. Afterwards he flew to Berlin to lead the coup.
47064.m: Claus von Stauffenberg carried out the assassination attempt of 20 July 1944.

47065.q: Where did the assassination attempt of 20 July 1944 take place?
a: At the Wolf's Lair in East Prussia
In the Reich Chancellery in Berlin
47065.e: The Wolf's Lair near Rastenburg in East Prussia was one of Hitler's headquarters. That day the briefing took place in a wooden hut and not in the bunker.
47065.m: The attempt of 20 July 1944 happened at the Wolf's Lair.

47066.q: Why did the coup attempt in Berlin collapse on the evening of 20 July 1944?
a: It became known that Hitler had survived
The Allies bombed the government district
The SS had discovered the plans weeks earlier
47066.e: As the news of Hitler's survival spread, many officers turned away from the conspirators. After a phone call with Hitler, Major Otto Ernst Remer had the coup put down.
47066.m: Hitler's survival made the coup of 20 July 1944 fail.

47067.q: Which circumstance contributed greatly to Hitler surviving the attempt of 20 July 1944?
a: The briefcase was moved behind a heavy table support
The bomb did not explode at all
Hitler left the room shortly before the explosion
The briefing took place in a concrete bunker
47067.e: An officer pushed the bag behind the heavy support of the map table, which shielded the blast. In addition, Stauffenberg had only been able to prime one of the two prepared explosive charges.
47067.m: A heavy table support and only one primed charge saved Hitler's life.

47068.q: What happened to Stauffenberg and several fellow conspirators in the night after the attempt of 20 July 1944?
a: They were put on trial in Nuremberg
They were freed by the Allies
47068.e: General Friedrich Fromm had Stauffenberg and other conspirators shot that same night in the courtyard of the Bendlerblock, probably to hide the fact that he had known about the plot.
47068.m: Stauffenberg was shot in the night of 20 July 1944.

47069.q: What was the plan called with which the conspirators of 20 July 1944 wanted to take power after the assassination?
47069.e: The “Valkyrie” plan was actually intended for internal unrest and was meant to mobilise the Replacement Army. The conspirators wanted to use it to put the party and the SS out of action after Hitler's death.
47069.m: The conspirators wanted to take power with the Valkyrie plan.

47070.q: Which former mayor of Leipzig had the conspirators chosen to be Reich Chancellor?
47070.e: Goerdeler was a central civilian figure of the conservative resistance. He was arrested after the failure and executed in 1945.
47070.m: Carl Goerdeler was to become Reich Chancellor after a coup.

47071.q: Which idea drove many of the 20 July 1944 conspirators, even though the war could hardly be turned around any more?
a: They wanted to show that there was another Germany
They wanted to win the war together with Hitler
They wanted to win the Soviet Union as an ally
They wanted to strengthen the Nazi Party
47071.e: Henning von Tresckow said, in essence, that practical success no longer mattered, only that the resistance had acted before the world. He took his own life on 21 July 1944.
47071.m: The resistance wanted to show that not all Germans stood behind Hitler.

47072.q: What was the job of Georg Elser, who tried to assassinate Hitler?
47072.e: Elser was a trained carpenter from Württemberg. His craft skills helped him build the bomb and its timer himself.
47072.m: Georg Elser was a craftsman and built his bomb himself.

47073.q: Where did Georg Elser set off a bomb on 8 November 1939 to kill Hitler?
47073.e: Hitler spoke there every year on the anniversary of the 1923 putsch. Elser had built the bomb into a pillar behind the speaker's platform.
47073.m: Georg Elser carried out his attack in Munich's Bürgerbräukeller.

47074.q: Why did Hitler survive Georg Elser's assassination attempt in November 1939?
a: He ended his speech earlier than planned
He did not come to the event at all
47074.e: Hitler left the hall about 13 minutes before the explosion because, due to the weather, he wanted to travel back by train instead of by plane. The bomb killed eight people.
47074.m: Hitler escaped Elser's bomb only because he left the hall early.

47075.q: Where was Georg Elser arrested on the evening of the attack?
a: At the Swiss border near Konstanz
At the French border near Strasbourg
In his home village of Königsbronn
47075.e: Elser wanted to flee to Switzerland near Konstanz. Customs officers stopped him even before the explosion and found suspicious items on him.
47075.m: Georg Elser was caught at the Swiss border while trying to escape.

47076.q: What is special about Georg Elser's assassination attempt compared with 20 July 1944?
a: He planned and acted completely alone
He was supported by the army
He was a senior party official
He acted on behalf of Britain
47076.e: Elser prepared the attack without anyone knowing and worked secretly in the hall for many nights. For a long time the Gestapo did not believe that a single person was behind it.
47076.m: Georg Elser acted alone, following his own conscience.

47077.q: When and where was Georg Elser murdered?
a: In April 1945 in Dachau concentration camp
In May 1945 in Mauthausen concentration camp
47077.e: Elser was held for years as a special prisoner in Sachsenhausen and Dachau. Shortly before the end of the war, on 9 April 1945, he was shot on orders from above.
47077.m: Georg Elser was murdered in Dachau a few weeks before the end of the war.

47078.q: How long was Georg Elser held after the attack before he was killed?
a: About five and a half years
47078.e: He was arrested in November 1939 and murdered in April 1945. The Nazi regime may have wanted to put him on show in a show trial after a victory.
47078.m: Georg Elser spent more than five years as a prisoner.

47079.e: Bonhoeffer was a Protestant theologian, pastor and university lecturer. He belonged to the Confessing Church, which opposed Nazi church policy.
47079.m: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Protestant theologian in the resistance.

47080.q: Which church movement, opposed to the Nazi “German Christians”, did Bonhoeffer belong to?
47080.e: The Confessing Church resisted the Nazi takeover of the Protestant church. Bonhoeffer ran its seminary for preachers in Finkenwalde.
47080.m: The Confessing Church resisted Nazi church policy.

47081.q: Through which authority did Bonhoeffer have contact with the military resistance?
47081.e: His brother-in-law Hans von Dohnanyi worked at the Abwehr under Wilhelm Canaris. Bonhoeffer was formally employed there and used trips abroad to make contacts for the resistance.
47081.m: Bonhoeffer was linked to the resistance through the Abwehr.

47082.q: Where was Dietrich Bonhoeffer executed on 9 April 1945?
47082.e: Bonhoeffer had been in prison since April 1943. A few weeks before the end of the war he was hanged in Flossenbürg concentration camp in the Upper Palatinate.
47082.m: Dietrich Bonhoeffer died shortly before the end of the war in Flossenbürg concentration camp.

47083.q: Which well-known poem did Bonhoeffer write in prison at the end of 1944?
47083.e: Bonhoeffer sent the poem as a Christmas greeting to his fiancée and his family in December 1944. It was later set to music and is now a frequently sung hymn.
47083.m: Bonhoeffer's poem about gracious powers was written in prison.

47084.q: Under which title were Bonhoeffer's letters and notes from prison published after the war?
47084.e: His friend Eberhard Bethge published the prison letters in 1951; the German title is “Widerstand und Ergebung”. The book is one of the most influential theological texts of the 20th century.
47084.m: Bonhoeffer's prison letters appeared as “Letters and Papers from Prison”.

47085.q: What did Bonhoeffer mean in 1933 by the church's task of “jamming a spoke in the wheel itself”?
a: Directly stopping the state when it does wrong
Only helping the victims through pastoral care
47085.e: Bonhoeffer argued that the church must help the victims, but in the most extreme case must also stop the unjust state. The sentence comes from his essay “The Church and the Jewish Question”.
47085.m: Bonhoeffer called for actively opposing the state's injustice.

47086.q: What was Nelson Mandela's profession before he went underground?
47086.e: In 1952 Mandela and Oliver Tambo opened the first law firm run by Black people in Johannesburg. They represented many victims of the apartheid laws.
47086.m: Nelson Mandela was a lawyer by profession.

47087.q: On which prison island did Nelson Mandela spend most of his imprisonment?
47087.e: Robben Island lies off Cape Town. Mandela was imprisoned there for 18 years before being moved to prisons on the mainland.
47087.m: Mandela was imprisoned for years on Robben Island off Cape Town.

47088.q: In which trial was Nelson Mandela sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964?
47088.e: In the Rivonia Trial, Mandela and other leaders of the armed resistance were charged with sabotage. In his speech in court he said he was prepared to die for the ideal of a free society.
47088.m: In the Rivonia Trial Mandela was given a life sentence.

47089.q: Which organisation did Mandela found in 1961 after the ANC had been banned?
a: The armed wing Umkhonto we Sizwe
47089.e: After the Sharpeville massacre and the ban on the ANC, Mandela no longer considered non-violent protest alone to be enough. Umkhonto we Sizwe means “Spear of the Nation” and mainly carried out acts of sabotage.
47089.m: Umkhonto we Sizwe was the armed wing of the ANC.

47090.q: By which clan name is Nelson Mandela often affectionately called in South Africa?
47090.e: Madiba is the name of his Xhosa clan. Many South Africans address him like this out of respect.
47090.m: Nelson Mandela is often called Madiba in South Africa.

47091.q: What is Nelson Mandela's autobiography called?
47091.e: Mandela began writing the book secretly in prison and published it in 1994. It was also made into a film in 2013.
47091.m: Mandela's autobiography is called “Long Walk to Freedom”.

47092.q: Which day has the UN declared Nelson Mandela International Day?
47092.e: In 2009 the UN General Assembly declared Mandela's birthday an international day. On this day people are encouraged to spend 67 minutes helping others, one minute for each year of his public service.
47092.m: Nelson Mandela Day is marked every year on 18 July.

47093.q: Which organisation did Alexei Navalny found in 2011 to expose corruption in Russia?
47093.e: The foundation, known as FBK, published investigations into the wealth of senior officials. In 2021 it was banned in Russia as “extremist”.
47093.m: Navalny exposed corruption in Russia with his foundation.

47094.q: In which Siberian city did the plane carrying the poisoned Navalny have to make an emergency landing in August 2020?
47094.e: The pilot made an unscheduled landing in Omsk, where Navalny was taken to hospital. This quick landing probably helped him survive.
47094.m: After the poisoning, Navalny's plane landed in Omsk.

47095.q: Which investigative platform, together with media partners, identified suspected intelligence agents who had followed Navalny in 2020?
47095.e: Bellingcat analysed phone and travel data together with The Insider, CNN and Der Spiegel. The investigation pointed to a team from the Russian FSB intelligence service.
47095.m: Bellingcat and its partners uncovered the suspected perpetrators in the Navalny case.

47096.q: Who is Alexei Navalny's wife, who announced after his death that she would continue his work?
47096.e: After her husband's death in 2024, Yulia Navalnaya appeared publicly as an opposition politician. She lives in exile.
47096.m: Yulia Navalnaya continues her husband's work.

47097.q: Which investigative video did Navalny's team publish in January 2021?
47097.e: The video describes a luxury complex on the Black Sea supposedly built for Vladimir Putin. Within a few days it had been viewed tens of millions of times.
47097.m: The video about a palace on the Black Sea reached a huge audience.

47098.q: In which election did Alexei Navalny surprisingly win about 27 per cent of the vote as a candidate in 2013?
47098.e: Navalny came second in the Moscow mayoral election behind the Kremlin-friendly incumbent. Later he was barred from presidential elections.
47098.m: Navalny achieved a strong result in the 2013 Moscow mayoral election.

47099.q: Which award did the documentary film “Navalny” receive in 2023?
47099.e: Among other things, the film shows Navalny getting a suspected participant in his poisoning to talk on the phone. It won its award at the 2023 Oscars.
47099.m: The film “Navalny” won an Oscar in 2023.

47100.q: Which book by Gene Sharp became a guide to non-violent resistance in many countries?
47100.e: Sharp originally wrote the book in 1993 for the democratic opposition in Burma. It has been translated into more than 30 languages.
47100.m: Gene Sharp's book “From Dictatorship to Democracy” is a guide to non-violent struggle.

47101.q: What did Gene Sharp collect in his main work of 1973?
a: A guide to armed guerrilla warfare
A history of the French Revolution
47101.e: In “The Politics of Nonviolent Action”, Sharp listed 198 methods, such as strikes, boycotts, sit-ins and symbolic protests. The list shows how varied non-violent resistance can be.
47101.m: Gene Sharp collected almost 200 methods of non-violent action.

47102.q: On which basic assumption is Gene Sharp's theory of power based?
a: Power depends on the cooperation of those who are ruled
Power rests only on military strength
47102.e: According to Sharp, even dictators need the obedience of officials, soldiers and the population. If this cooperation is refused on a mass scale, their power collapses.
47102.m: No ruler can govern without the cooperation of many people.

47103.q: Into which three main groups did Gene Sharp divide the methods of non-violent action?
47103.e: Protest and persuasion include demonstrations, for example. Non-cooperation means strikes and boycotts; non-violent intervention means things like blockades or occupations.
47103.m: Sharp grouped non-violent methods into protest, non-cooperation and intervention.

47104.q: What did Gene Sharp call “political jiu-jitsu”?
a: Violence against non-violent people weakens the oppressor itself
Opponents are outwitted through secret deals
Protesters defend themselves with martial arts
Governments fight the opposition with laws
47104.e: When a regime brutally attacks peaceful people, it often loses support among the population, the security forces and abroad. In this way the opponent's strength is turned against it.
47104.m: In political jiu-jitsu, the regime's violence harms the regime itself.

47105.q: Why did Gene Sharp consider non-violent resistance against dictatorships wiser than armed struggle?
a: When it comes to violence, a regime is usually stronger
Non-violent resistance always reaches its goal faster
Dictators are not allowed to arrest non-violent people
Armed struggle is always forbidden under international law
47105.e: Dictatorships have an army, police and weapons. Anyone who fights them with violence attacks them where they are strongest; non-violent methods, by contrast, target their weak points.
47105.m: Sharp advised not to attack a dictatorship where it is strongest.

47106.q: Which Serbian youth movement, which helped bring down Slobodan Milošević in 2000, relied on Gene Sharp's ideas?
47106.e: Otpor! means “Resistance!” and relied on humour, symbols and mass protest. Its methods were later taken up by movements in other countries.
47106.m: The Serbian movement Otpor! used Gene Sharp's strategies.

47107.q: What does lustration mean in politics?
a: Checking officials for involvement with the former regime
Dissolving a parliament before new elections
47107.e: After communist regimes ended, applicants for public office were checked to see whether they had, for example, worked with the secret police. People found to be compromised could be excluded from certain posts.
47107.m: Lustration means checking public office holders for links to the dictatorship.

47108.q: What does the Latin word “lustratio”, from which the term lustration comes, mean?
47108.e: In ancient Rome the lustratio was a purification sacrifice. The political term applies this idea to “cleaning up” state institutions.
47108.m: Lustration comes from the Latin word for purification.

47109.q: Which country passed a comprehensive lustration law in 1991, one of the first in Central Europe?
47109.e: The Czechoslovak law excluded former state security staff and senior party officials from certain state offices. It was considered particularly strict.
47109.m: Czechoslovakia introduced a strict lustration law in 1991.

47110.q: How does lustration fundamentally differ from a criminal trial?
a: It controls access to offices, not punishment
It always leads to a prison sentence
It is only carried out by international courts
It only concerns people who have died
47110.e: Lustration is an administrative procedure that checks suitability for certain positions. No criminal guilt has to be established for it.
47110.m: Lustration excludes people from offices but does not punish them in the criminal sense.

47111.q: Which state institution in Poland is responsible for dealing with communist crimes and the lustration files?
47111.e: The Institute of National Remembrance, IPN in Polish, manages the files of the former state security service. It also carries out historical research and criminal investigations.
47111.m: In Poland the Institute of National Remembrance manages the secret police files.

47112.q: Which criticism is often made of lustration procedures?
a: Incomplete secret service files can incriminate innocent people
They are too cheap for the state
47112.e: Secret service files can be incomplete, forged or one-sided. Critics therefore warn of collective guilt and political misuse.
47112.m: Lustration is controversial because secret service files are not always reliable.

47113.q: Which country passed a lustration law after the Euromaidan in 2014?
47113.e: The law was meant to remove officials from President Yanukovych's time and former KGB staff from the civil service. Internationally it was partly criticised as going too far.
47113.m: Ukraine carried out lustration after the Euromaidan in 2014.

47114.q: Who led South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
47114.e: The Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize winner Desmond Tutu led the commission from 1996. He shaped its focus on reconciliation.
47114.m: Desmond Tutu led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

47115.q: Which period did South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission investigate?
47115.e: The period began in March 1960, the month of the Sharpeville massacre. It ended when Mandela took office in May 1994.
47115.m: The commission investigated human rights violations from 1960 to 1994.

47116.q: Which three committees made up the Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
47116.e: One committee heard victims, one decided on amnesty applications and one proposed reparation and rehabilitation. In this way victims and perpetrators were dealt with separately.
47116.m: The commission worked with three committees.

47117.q: Which idea of justice mainly underlay the work of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
47117.e: Instead of punishment, the focus was on healing victims and society, often linked to the African concept of ubuntu. Experts call this “restorative justice”.
47117.m: The commission relied on restorative rather than retributive justice.

47118.q: What could perpetrators receive from South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission if they fully disclosed their politically motivated acts?
47118.e: The conditions were a full confession and a political motive. Of around 7,000 applications only a small share, about 850, were granted.
47118.m: Only a small share of the amnesty applications were granted.

47119.q: Which law formed the basis for South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 1995?
a: The Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act
47119.e: The Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act was passed in 1995. The commission presented its final report in 1998.
47119.m: A law of 1995 created the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

47120.q: What happened in 2021 to the independent Stasi Records Agency and its files?
a: The files were transferred to the Federal Archives
The files were handed over to Russia
47120.e: On 17 June 2021 the independent Stasi Records Agency was dissolved. The files were transferred to the Federal Archives and remain accessible.
47120.m: Since 2021 the Stasi Records Archive has been part of the Federal Archives.

47121.q: Who was the first Federal Commissioner for the Stasi Records?
47121.e: Joachim Gauck led the agency from 1990 to 2000, which is why people called it the “Gauck Authority”. He later became Federal President.
47121.m: The Stasi Records Agency was also called the Gauck Authority after its first head.

47122.q: Roughly how long would the files of the Stasi Records Archive be if they were lined up end to end?
47122.e: Over decades the Stasi collected huge amounts of files, index cards, photos and sound recordings. The written documents alone come to about 111 kilometres.
47122.m: The Stasi files fill about 111 kilometres of shelves.

47123.q: From when could citizens see their own Stasi files?
47123.e: The Stasi Records Act came into force at the end of December 1991. Since 2 January 1992 the people concerned have been able to apply to see their files.
47123.m: Since 1992 people have been able to read their Stasi files.

47124.q: What is kept in about 15,000 sacks in the Stasi Records Archive?
a: Torn-up files that are to be reconstructed
47124.e: During the upheaval of 1989 and 1990 the Stasi tried to tear up and destroy files by hand. Since then the scraps have been painstakingly pieced together by hand and with computers.
47124.m: Thousands of sacks of torn Stasi files are waiting to be reconstructed.

47125.q: What did the Stasi call people who secretly gave it information about others?
47125.e: These so-called IMs spied on friends, colleagues and even family members. Their reports are a central part of the Stasi files.
47125.m: Unofficial collaborators spied on the people around them for the Stasi.

47126.q: What did civil rights activists do at the Stasi headquarters in Berlin in January 1990?
a: They occupied it to secure the files
They sold the files to the West
They set up a new parliament there
47126.e: The headquarters of the Ministry for State Security was on Normannenstrasse in Berlin-Lichtenberg. Activists occupied the site on 15 January 1990 to stop more files being destroyed.
47126.m: In 1990 civil rights activists saved many files from destruction at the Stasi headquarters.

47127.q: Which artist started the Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) project?
47127.e: The Cologne artist Gunter Demnig started the project in the 1990s. He lays many of the stones himself.
47127.m: Gunter Demnig created the stumbling stones.

47128.q: What is the visible surface of a stumbling stone made of?
47128.e: A brass plate is fixed on a small concrete cube, with the name and life dates stamped into it. The stone is set flush into the pavement.
47128.m: Stumbling stones carry a brass plate with a victim's details.

47129.q: Where are stumbling stones usually laid?
a: Outside the victim's last freely chosen home
In the cemetery of their home town
At the place of death in the concentration camp
47129.e: The stones are placed where people last lived of their own free will before they were persecuted. That is why many inscriptions begin with “Here lived”.
47129.m: A stumbling stone lies outside a victim's last freely chosen home.

47130.q: Because of its size, what is the stumbling stones project regarded as today?
a: The largest decentralised memorial in the world
The only memorial under UN protection
47130.e: Since May 2023 there have been more than 100,000 stumbling stones in many European countries. They are spread across thousands of places instead of one single site.
47130.m: The stumbling stones form the largest decentralised memorial in the world.

47131.q: Where were the first stumbling stones in Switzerland laid in 2013?
47131.e: On 8 September 2013 the first two stumbling stones in Switzerland were laid in Kreuzlingen in the canton of Thurgau. Other places such as Zurich, Basel, Bern and St Gallen followed later.
47131.m: The first Swiss stumbling stones are in Kreuzlingen.

47132.q: Which large German city decided in 2015 not to allow stumbling stones on public ground?
47132.e: Munich's city council decided against stumbling stones on public streets, partly because critics found it undignified to step on names. Instead the city uses its own memorial plaques on house walls.
47132.m: Munich only allows stumbling stones on private ground.

a: A long memorial plate for many victims at one place
A stumbling stone for a single person
A memorial plaque on a house wall
A monument in the shape of a gate
47133.e: Stumbling thresholds are brass plates about a metre long. They remember, for example, groups of people who were deported from or turned away at a particular place.
47133.m: A stumbling threshold remembers many victims at once.

47134.q: Which office did Paul Grüninger hold when he helped Jewish refugees in 1938?
a: Police commander of the canton of St Gallen
47134.e: Grüninger was commander of the St Gallen cantonal police. In this role he was also responsible for refugees on the border with Austria.
47134.m: Paul Grüninger was police commander in St Gallen.

47135.q: How did Paul Grüninger allow refugees to stay legally in Switzerland in 1938 and 1939?
a: He backdated their entry to before the border was closed
He hid them in police stations
He sent them by train to France
47135.e: After the border was closed in August 1938, refugees without a visa were no longer allowed in. Grüninger entered earlier dates of entry and so gave several hundred people the right to stay.
47135.m: Grüninger saved refugees with backdated entry dates.

47136.q: What consequences did helping refugees have for Paul Grüninger himself?
a: He had to go to prison in Germany
47136.e: Grüninger was dismissed without notice in 1939 and lost his pension. In 1940 a court convicted him of breach of official duty; afterwards he lived in poverty.
47136.m: Because of his humanity, Paul Grüninger lost his job and his pension.

47137.q: In which year was Paul Grüninger acquitted after his death by the St Gallen district court?
47137.e: The court overturned the 1940 verdict 23 years after Grüninger's death. The St Gallen government had already rehabilitated him politically in 1993.
47137.m: Paul Grüninger was legally rehabilitated in 1995.

47138.q: Which honour did Paul Grüninger receive in 1971 from the Israeli memorial Yad Vashem?
a: A nomination for the Nobel Peace Prize
47138.e: Yad Vashem honours non-Jews who saved Jews at the risk of their lives or at great sacrifice. Grüninger received the title during his lifetime, a year before he died.
47138.m: Paul Grüninger was honoured as Righteous Among the Nations.

47139.q: Which football stadium in St Gallen has been named after Paul Grüninger since 2006?
a: The Kybunpark of FC St Gallen
47139.e: As a young man Grüninger played for SC Brühl and won the Swiss championship with the club in 1915. Later he was also its president.
47139.m: The Paul Grüninger Stadium belongs to SC Brühl in St Gallen.

47140.q: What is the 2014 docudrama about Paul Grüninger called?
47140.e: The film by Alain Gsponer, whose title means “The Grüninger File”, shows the investigation into Grüninger in 1938. It was shown in Swiss cinemas in 2014.
47140.m: The film “Akte Grüninger” tells the story of the St Gallen police commander.

47141.q: In which city did the Swiss diplomat Carl Lutz save tens of thousands of Jews during the Second World War?
47141.e: Carl Lutz was vice-consul in Budapest and issued letters of protection from 1942. Before that he had worked in Jaffa in Palestine.
47141.m: Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of people in Budapest.

47142.q: With which documents did Carl Lutz protect Jews from deportation?
47142.e: Lutz issued letters of protection that placed their holders under Swiss protection. They were originally meant for emigrants to Palestine, but he greatly extended them.
47142.m: Carl Lutz saved people with Swiss letters of protection.

47143.q: Roughly how many people is Carl Lutz said to have saved?
47143.e: Lutz is credited with saving about 62,000 Hungarian Jews. This is considered one of the largest civilian rescue operations of the Second World War.
47143.m: Carl Lutz saved the lives of about 62,000 people.

47144.q: What was the well-known building in Budapest that Carl Lutz turned into a protected refuge called?
47144.e: The Glass House was a former glass factory that counted as a branch of the Swiss legation. Thousands of people found shelter there.
47144.m: The Glass House in Budapest was a refuge under Swiss protection.

47145.q: How did the Swiss authorities first react to Carl Lutz's actions after the war?
a: They accused him of exceeding his authority
They gave him the Federal Cross of Merit
They stripped him of his citizenship
47145.e: An inquiry found his conduct correct but described the protective papers as going beyond his powers. Only in 1995 was he rehabilitated after his death by the Federal Council.
47145.m: Carl Lutz was only properly honoured in Switzerland much later.

47146.q: Which institution awards the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought?
47146.e: The European Parliament has awarded the prize every year since 1988. The ceremony usually takes place in Strasbourg in December.
47146.m: The Sakharov Prize is awarded by the European Parliament.

47147.q: Who is the Sakharov Prize named after?
a: The Soviet physicist and dissident Andrei Sakharov
The Polish trade unionist Lech Wałęsa
47147.e: Andrei Sakharov was a nuclear physicist who later campaigned for human rights in the Soviet Union. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975.
47147.m: The prize honours the memory of the civil rights campaigner Andrei Sakharov.

47148.q: How much prize money does the Sakharov Prize carry (as of 2025)?
47148.e: The prize is worth 50,000 euros. Often the international attention for the winners matters more than the money.
47148.m: The Sakharov Prize is worth 50,000 euros.

47149.q: Who received the Sakharov Prize in 1988 as one of the first winners, even though he was in prison at the time?
47149.e: The first Sakharov Prize went in 1988 to the imprisoned Nelson Mandela and, after his death, to the Soviet dissident Anatoly Marchenko. Mandela was only released in 1990.
47149.m: Nelson Mandela was one of the first Sakharov Prize winners.

47150.q: To whom did the European Parliament award the Sakharov Prize in 2022?
47150.e: The prize honoured the resistance to Russia's war of aggression. President Zelensky, elected representatives and civil society were named as representatives.
47150.m: The 2022 Sakharov Prize went to the Ukrainian people.

47151.q: Who received the Sakharov Prize in 2023?
a: Jina Mahsa Amini and the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement
47151.e: Jina Mahsa Amini died in 2022 in the custody of Iran's morality police. Her death sparked nationwide protests, which the Parliament honoured with the prize.
47151.m: The 2023 Sakharov Prize honoured the Iranian women's movement.

47152.q: Which Venezuelan opposition politicians received the Sakharov Prize in 2024?
a: María Corina Machado and Edmundo González
47152.e: The Parliament honoured the two for their efforts for free elections in Venezuela. González had been a candidate in the disputed presidential election in July 2024.
47152.m: The 2024 Sakharov Prize went to the Venezuelan opposition.

47153.q: Who used the term “historical materialism” for Marx's view of history and made it well known?
47153.e: Marx himself did not speak of “historical materialism”. Engels used the expression from about 1890 in letters and writings, after which it became widely accepted.
47153.m: The term “historical materialism” became known mainly through Friedrich Engels.

47154.q: According to the “Communist Manifesto”, the history of all society so far is the history of what?
47154.e: The 1848 Manifesto opens its first section with this sentence. For Marx and Engels, conflict between classes drives history forward.
47154.m: According to Marx and Engels, class struggles drive history forward.

47155.q: Whose idealist dialectics did Marx and Engels want to “turn upside down” in a materialist way?
47155.e: For Hegel, the mind develops dialectically. Marx took over the method but put material conditions first.
47155.m: Marx took over Hegel's dialectics and reinterpreted it in a materialist way.

47156.q: According to Marx, with what do the productive forces come into conflict, so that an era of social revolution begins?
a: With the size of the population
With the supply of raw materials
47156.e: According to Marx, growing productive forces eventually burst the existing property and production relations. This leads to an upheaval of society.
47156.m: According to Marx, revolutions arise from the conflict between productive forces and relations of production.

47157.q: In the classic scheme of historical materialism, which form of society follows feudalism?
47157.e: The scheme is primitive society, slave society, feudalism, capitalism and finally socialism or communism.
47157.m: In the Marxist scheme of history, capitalism replaces feudalism.

47158.q: According to Marx, what mainly determines people's consciousness?
a: The economic conditions they live in
47158.e: In 1859 Marx wrote: “It is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but, on the contrary, their social being that determines their consciousness.” This is the core of historical materialism.
47158.m: According to Marx, social being determines consciousness.

47159.q: In which notes of 1845 is the sentence that philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways, but the point is to change it?
47159.e: It is the eleventh of the eleven short theses. Engels published them in 1888 as an appendix to his work on Feuerbach.
47159.m: The eleventh thesis on Feuerbach calls not just for interpreting the world but for changing it.

47160.q: Which two thinkers developed the materialist view of history together?
a: Karl Marx and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Immanuel Kant and Johann Gottlieb Fichte
47160.e: Marx and Engels worked closely together from 1844, for example on “The German Ideology” and the “Communist Manifesto”. They took dialectics from Hegel but reinterpreted it in a materialist way.
47160.m: Marx and Engels founded historical materialism together.

47161.q: According to Marx, what is the real purpose of capitalist production?
a: To turn money into more money
47161.e: The capitalist uses money to buy goods such as raw materials and labour power and sells the products for more money. Marx summed this up in the formula M-C-M'.
47161.m: For Marx, capital is money that is meant to become more money.

47162.q: According to Marx, what alone creates new value and therefore surplus value?
47162.e: According to Marx, machines and raw materials only pass on their own value to the product. Only labour power creates more value than it costs itself.
47162.m: According to Marx, only human labour power creates more value than it costs.

47163.q: A worker works 10 hours a day. She has produced the value of her wage after 4 hours. According to Marx, how many hours of surplus labour does she perform?
47163.e: Marx calls the time in which she produces the value of her wage necessary labour. The rest, here 10 minus 4 equals 6 hours, is taken by the capitalist as surplus value.
47163.m: Surplus labour is the working time beyond the value of the wage.

47164.q: According to Marx, how can a capitalist increase surplus value most directly without changing wages?
a: By making the working day longer
47164.e: If the time needed for the wage stays the same and the working day gets longer, surplus labour grows. Marx calls this absolute surplus value.
47164.m: According to Marx, a longer working day increases surplus value.

47165.q: According to Marx, why does surplus value rise when food becomes cheaper thanks to better technology?
a: Labour power becomes cheaper, so surplus labour grows
The state pays the factories subsidies
47165.e: If the cost of living falls, the value of labour power falls. With a working day of the same length, more time is left for surplus labour. Marx calls this relative surplus value.
47165.m: According to Marx, cheaper food shortens the necessary working time.

47166.q: According to Marx, what does the worker actually sell to the capitalist?
47166.e: Marx distinguishes between labour power and labour. The value of labour power is paid for, but the labour itself creates more value, and this difference is surplus value.
47166.m: According to Marx, the wage worker sells his labour power, not his labour.

47167.q: The rate of profit is the profit divided by all the capital used. A business uses 600 francs for machines and raw materials and 200 francs for wages and makes 200 francs profit. What is the rate of profit?
47167.e: The total capital used is 600 + 200 = 800 francs. 200 divided by 800 gives 0.25, which is 25 per cent.
47167.m: The rate of profit measures profit against all the capital used.

47168.q: Which law in Marx says that the rate of profit falls in the long run because the share of constant capital grows?
a: Law of the tendency of the rate of profit to fall
47168.e: Marx describes it in the third volume of “Das Kapital”. If more and more is invested in machines and less and less in labour power, surplus value falls in relation to total capital.
47168.m: According to Marx, the rate of profit in capitalism tends to fall in the long run.

47169.q: What did Marx call the state in the transition period from capitalism to communism?
47169.e: In the “Critique of the Gotha Programme” of 1875, Marx describes a political transition period in which the working class holds power. Only after that would the classless society follow.
47169.m: For Marx, the path to communism leads through the dictatorship of the proletariat.

47170.q: Which event did Engels explicitly call an example of the dictatorship of the proletariat in 1891?
47170.e: In his introduction to “The Civil War in France”, Engels wrote, in essence, that people should look at the Paris Commune: that was the dictatorship of the proletariat.
47170.m: Engels saw the Paris Commune as a model of the dictatorship of the proletariat.

47171.q: According to Engels, what happens to the state once class differences have disappeared?
47171.e: In “Anti-Dühring”, Engels writes that the state is not abolished, it withers away. Without classes, there is no need for a machine of oppression any more.
47171.m: According to Engels, the state becomes unnecessary in a classless society and withers away.

47172.q: In which work of 1917 did Lenin set out in detail his view of the state and the dictatorship of the proletariat?
47172.e: Lenin wrote the work in the summer and autumn of 1917, partly while hiding in Finland. He relied heavily on Marx's writings on the Paris Commune.
47172.m: Lenin's “The State and Revolution” explains his theory of the proletarian state.

47173.q: In 1852, what did Marx consider to be his own new contribution to class theory?
a: Showing that class struggle leads to the dictatorship of the proletariat
47173.e: In a letter to Joseph Weydemeyer, Marx stressed that others had described classes before him. What was new in his work was the link between class struggle, the dictatorship of the proletariat and the classless society.
47173.m: Marx saw his contribution in linking class struggle with the goal of a classless society.

47174.q: According to Marx, what marks the proletariat as a class?
a: It owns no means of production
47174.e: Proletarians own neither factories nor land and therefore have to sell their labour power for wages. The bourgeoisie, by contrast, owns the means of production.
47174.m: Proletarians own no means of production and live by selling their labour power.

47175.q: Who were called “proletarii” in ancient Rome, from which the word “proletariat” comes?
a: The poorest citizens, who owned only their offspring
The slaves on the country estates
47175.e: The Latin “proles” means offspring. The poorest citizens could give the state nothing but their children.
47175.m: The word proletariat goes back to the poorest citizens of ancient Rome.

47176.q: Which Western European communist party dropped the dictatorship of the proletariat from its aims in 1976?
a: The Communist Party of the Soviet Union
47176.e: Under Georges Marchais, the party gave up the term at its 22nd congress. This was part of so-called Eurocommunism, which distanced itself from Moscow.
47176.m: In Eurocommunism, Western parties gave up the dictatorship of the proletariat as a goal.

47177.q: According to Marx, what forms the “base” of a society?
a: All the relations of production together
47177.e: The economic structure, meaning how things are produced and distributed and who owns the means of production, is the real base. The superstructure rises on top of it.
47177.m: For Marx, economic relations form the base of society.

47178.q: According to Marx, which area belongs to the superstructure?
a: The division of labour in a business
47178.e: The superstructure includes law, the state, politics, religion, philosophy and art. Machines and working relations belong to the economic level.
47178.m: According to Marx, law, politics, religion and art belong to the superstructure.

47179.q: According to Marx, what determines people's consciousness?
47179.e: In his preface of 1859, Marx writes that consciousness does not determine being, but social being determines consciousness.
47179.m: According to Marx, living conditions shape the way people think.

47180.q: How did Engels tone down the role of the economy in a letter to Joseph Bloch in 1890?
a: It was only decisive “in the last instance”
It was merely a part of religion
47180.e: Engels stressed that elements of the superstructure also have an effect on the course of history. Anyone who made the economy the only decisive factor was twisting the theory.
47180.m: Engels stressed that the economy is only decisive in the last instance.

47181.q: What did the philosopher Louis Althusser mean by “ideological state apparatuses”?
a: Institutions such as schools, churches and the media that pass on values
47181.e: In 1970 Althusser distinguished these institutions from the police and the army. They secure power not through force but through ideology.
47181.m: Louis Althusser studied how schools and the media spread ideology.

47182.q: What did Marx call religion in 1844?
47182.e: The phrase appears in the introduction to “A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right”. Religion comforts people in their misery without removing its causes.
47182.m: Marx saw religion as a comfort that makes misery bearable but does not remove it.

47183.q: According to Marx and Engels, whose ideas are the ruling ideas in every era?
47183.e: According to Marx and Engels, the class that controls the material means of production also controls the means of mental production. In this way it shapes the dominant ideas.
47183.m: According to Marx, those who rule economically also decide the dominant ideas.

47184.q: What does Marx describe with the term “alienated labour”?
a: The worker does not recognise himself in his work and its product
The worker earns more than he needs
The worker owns the factory himself
