47184.e: In the Paris Manuscripts of 1844 Marx shows that the product belongs to the capitalist and the activity is decided by others. So work becomes something foreign to the worker.
47184.m: According to Marx, alienated labour is work decided by others, whose product does not belong to the worker.

47185.q: According to Marx, besides the product, the activity and his species-being, from whom else is the worker alienated?
47185.e: Marx describes four forms of alienation. Anyone who is alienated from their own nature is also a stranger to their fellow human beings.
47185.m: According to Marx, wage labour also alienates people from their fellow human beings.

47186.q: From which philosopher did Marx take the term “species-being”?
47186.e: Feuerbach described the human being as a species-being that is aware of its own nature. Marx linked the term with free, creative work.
47186.m: The term species-being comes from Ludwig Feuerbach.

47187.q: In “Das Kapital”, what does Marx call the fact that social relations appear as properties of things?
47187.e: Value seems to be a property of the commodity itself. But behind it are relationships between people who produce for each other.
47187.m: In commodity fetishism, human relationships appear as relationships between things.

47188.q: What does the term “reification” mean in Marxist philosophy?
a: Relationships between people appear as relationships between things
People collect more and more things
Goods are distributed by the state
47188.e: The term was coined by the Hungarian philosopher György Lukács in 1923. He built on Marx's idea of commodity fetishism.
47188.m: Reification means that human relationships appear as relationships between things.

47189.q: According to Marx's Paris Manuscripts, where does the worker only feel “at home”?
47189.e: Marx writes that the worker only feels at home outside work and feels outside himself at work. For him, work is only a means of survival.
47189.m: According to Marx, the worker experiences alienated labour as foreign and forced.

47190.q: In which work by Hegel from 1807 does the alienation of spirit play an important role?
47190.e: Hegel describes how spirit externalises itself and finds itself again in a foreign world. Marx applied this idea to work.
47190.m: Marx took the concept of alienation from Hegel in a changed form.

47191.q: In which Scottish village did Robert Owen run a cotton mill as a model social community?
47191.e: There Owen shortened working hours, improved housing and limited child labour. The village is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
47191.m: Robert Owen turned New Lanark into a model social factory.

47192.q: What were people supposed to pay with at Robert Owen's London exchange of 1832?
47192.e: At the “National Equitable Labour Exchange”, goods were valued by the working time they contained. The notes were meant to replace money, but the project only lasted a short time.
47192.m: Owen wanted goods to be exchanged according to the working time put into them.

47193.q: Which institution for young children did Owen open in his model community in 1816?
47193.e: The “Infant School” is regarded as one of the first schools for young children in Britain. Owen was convinced that environment and education shape character.
47193.m: Owen believed that good education shapes people from early childhood.

47194.q: What did Charles Fourier call the communal buildings of his ideal society?
47194.e: In the phalanstère, people were to live and work together. Fourier wanted to share out work according to people's inclinations so that it would be enjoyable.
47194.m: Fourier planned the phalanstère as a community for living and working.

47195.q: How did Charles Fourier want to make work in his community enjoyable?
a: Everyone would work according to their inclinations and change activity often
Through machines that do all the work
47195.e: Fourier believed that people like to work if the work suits their passions. So they were to switch between activities several times a day.
47195.m: Fourier wanted to share out work according to inclinations.

47196.q: Which French count is regarded, alongside Owen and Fourier, as the third classic figure of early socialism?
47196.e: Saint-Simon wanted a society led by industrialists and scientists. His followers formed their own movement, the Saint-Simonians.
47196.m: Saint-Simon, Fourier and Owen are regarded as the classic figures of early socialism.

47197.q: In which work did Engels contrast “utopian” with “scientific” socialism?
47197.e: The 1880 work is an extract from “Anti-Dühring”. Engels praised the early socialists but criticised them for not analysing society scientifically.
47197.m: Engels distinguished utopian from scientific socialism.

47198.q: Which German journeyman tailor and early socialist was arrested in Zurich in 1843?
47198.e: In Switzerland Weitling campaigned among craftsmen for a communism shaped by Christianity. The Zurich authorities arrested him and later expelled him.
47198.m: Wilhelm Weitling also spread his early communist ideas in Switzerland.

47199.q: Which Russian anarchist founded his own group in Geneva in 1868 and became Marx's great opponent?
47199.e: In 1868 Bakunin founded the Alliance of Socialist Democracy in Geneva. The dispute with Marx led to the split of the International in 1872.
47199.m: Mikhail Bakunin was Marx's anarchist opponent.

47200.q: Why was Bakunin expelled from the First International in 1872?
a: Because of his power struggle with Marx and his followers
Because of spying for the Tsar
Because he had become a Swiss citizen
Because he urged workers to vote
47200.e: Marx and his followers accused Bakunin of infiltrating the International with a secret organisation. James Guillaume from the Neuchâtel Jura was expelled with him.
47200.m: In 1872 the International expelled Bakunin after the dispute with Marx.

47201.q: Why did many German revolutionaries live in Switzerland, for example in Geneva, in the mid-19th century?
a: They had fled after the failed revolutions of 1848/49
47201.e: After the uprisings of 1848 and 1849 many revolutionaries fled to Switzerland. One of them, Johann Philipp Becker, built up the German-speaking sections of the International from Geneva.
47201.m: In the 19th century Switzerland was a refuge for revolutionaries.

47202.q: In which Swiss city did the 1869 congress of the International take place, at which Bakunin's followers were very prominent?
47202.e: At the congress there was a dispute about abolishing the right of inheritance. The conflict between Marx and Bakunin became clearly visible there.
47202.m: The Basel congress of 1869 showed the dispute between Marxists and anarchists.

47203.q: Why did the First International fall apart after 1872?
a: Because of the dispute between Marxists and anarchists
Because it was banned by the League of Nations
Because all its aims had been achieved
Because all members joined the SPD
47203.e: After the split of 1872 and the move of the General Council to New York, the organisation quickly lost importance. It was formally dissolved in Philadelphia in 1876.
47203.m: The dispute between Marx and Bakunin led to the end of the First International.

47204.q: What was the anarchist-minded association of watchmakers in the Swiss Jura that sided with Bakunin called?
47204.e: The watchmakers often worked in small workshops and valued self-management. The federation became a centre of anarchism in Europe.
47204.m: The Jura Federation made the Swiss Jura a centre of anarchism.

47205.q: In which town in the Bernese Jura was the anti-authoritarian International founded in 1872?
47205.e: After Bakunin's expulsion, his followers met in Saint-Imier in September 1872. The congress is regarded as the birth of the anarchist movement.
47205.m: The anti-authoritarian International was founded in Saint-Imier in 1872.

47206.q: To which city did the Hague Congress of 1872 move the General Council of the International?
47206.e: Marx wanted to remove the General Council from the influence of Bakunin's followers. After that the organisation quickly lost importance.
47206.m: With the move of the General Council to New York, the First International came to an end.

47207.q: Roughly how long did the Paris Commune of 1871 last?
47207.e: It began on 18 March 1871 and ended on 28 May 1871. Government troops recaptured Paris.
47207.m: The Paris Commune lasted only about two and a half months.

47208.q: What did the government want to do on Montmartre on 18 March 1871, when the Commune uprising began?
47208.e: The people of Paris had paid for the guns with their own money and wanted to keep them. Soldiers joined the crowd, and the government withdrew to Versailles.
47208.m: The dispute over the cannons on Montmartre set off the Paris Commune.

47209.q: Who led the French government in Versailles that moved against the Commune?
47209.e: Thiers was head of the executive of the new republic. He had Paris recaptured by government troops.
47209.m: Adolphe Thiers had the Paris Commune crushed by military force.

47210.q: How did the Paris Commune end in May 1871?
a: Government troops recaptured Paris in a bloody week
The Commune dissolved peacefully after elections
The Communards took over all of France
47210.e: During the “Bloody Week” at the end of May 1871, government troops fought street by street. Thousands of Communards were killed, many of them shot.
47210.m: The Paris Commune was bloodily crushed in 1871.

47211.q: Which measure did the Commune decide on for bakeries?
a: A ban on bread on Sundays
47211.e: The decree of April 1871 was meant to improve the harsh working conditions of journeyman bakers.
47211.m: The Paris Commune banned night work in bakeries.

47212.q: Which painter was blamed for pulling down the Vendôme Column and then fled to Switzerland?
47212.e: Courbet was supposed to pay for rebuilding the column. He lived in La Tour-de-Peilz on Lake Geneva until his death in 1877.
47212.m: After the Commune, Gustave Courbet spent his last years on Lake Geneva.

47213.q: Which teacher and fighter of the Commune was banished to New Caledonia?
47213.e: Louise Michel fought on the barricades and defended herself openly in court. After returning in 1880 she remained a well-known anarchist.
47213.m: Louise Michel became the best-known woman of the Paris Commune.

47214.q: In which work of 1902 did Lenin call for a party of professional revolutionaries?
47214.e: Lenin wanted a tightly organised, disciplined cadre party. As a vanguard it was to lead the working class to revolution.
47214.m: In “What Is to Be Done?” Lenin set out the idea of the vanguard party.

47215.q: According to Lenin, what kind of consciousness do workers develop on their own, without a party?
47215.e: Lenin believed that workers by themselves only fight over wages and working hours. Socialist consciousness had to be brought in from outside by the party.
47215.m: According to Lenin, the party brings revolutionary consciousness into the working class from outside.

47216.q: What does the Russian name “Bolsheviks” mean when translated?
47216.e: At the congress of the Russian Social Democrats in 1903, Lenin's wing won an important vote. Its opponents were then called Mensheviks, meaning those of the minority.
47216.m: The Bolsheviks named themselves after a majority at the 1903 party congress.

47217.q: What is Lenin's organisational principle called, under which the leadership's decisions are binding on all members?
47217.e: Discussion was to be allowed before a decision, but after it strict discipline applied. In practice this led to rule by the party leadership.
47217.m: Democratic centralism binds all party members to the leadership's decisions.

47218.q: In which work of 1920 did Lenin criticise left communists who wanted to boycott parliaments and trade unions?
47218.e: Lenin advised the young communist parties in the West to work in parliaments and trade unions too. He considered pure refusal immature.
47218.m: Lenin rejected boycotting parliaments and trade unions as an infantile disorder.

47219.q: Which slogan was at the centre of Lenin's April Theses of 1917?
47219.e: After returning to Petrograd, Lenin demanded that the Provisional Government should not be supported. Power was to go to the councils.
47219.m: In the April Theses Lenin demanded power for the councils.

47220.q: Which organisation did the Bolsheviks found in Moscow in 1919 to push forward world revolution?
47220.e: It is called the Comintern for short. Its member parties had to submit to strict instructions from Moscow.
47220.m: With the Comintern, Lenin wanted to direct communist parties around the world.

47221.q: Under which ruler did “Marxism-Leninism” become the official state ideology of the Soviet Union?
47221.e: After Lenin's death in 1924, Stalin systematised his teachings. The term became the basis of the ideology of all Eastern Bloc parties.
47221.m: Stalin made Marxism-Leninism the compulsory state doctrine.

47222.q: What does Trotsky's theory of permanent revolution say?
a: The revolution must go beyond the bourgeois stage and continue internationally
Revolutions repeat themselves every hundred years
Every government must be overthrown each year
The revolution should only happen peacefully and slowly
47222.e: Even in backward countries the working class must take power. But socialism is only possible if the revolution spreads to other countries.
47222.m: According to Trotsky, a revolution must not stay limited to one country.

47223.q: Which doctrine of Stalin opposed Trotsky's permanent revolution?
47223.e: From 1924 Stalin argued that the Soviet Union could build socialism on its own. Trotsky saw this as a break with internationalism.
47223.m: Stalin relied on socialism in one country, Trotsky on world revolution.

47224.q: Which army did Trotsky build up from 1918 as People's Commissar for War?
47224.e: During the civil war Trotsky formed the Red Army from volunteers and conscripts. The Whites were its opponents; the other armies belonged to China and East Germany.
47224.m: Trotsky was the founder of the Red Army.

47225.q: In which year did Trotsky found the Fourth International?
47225.e: The founding conference took place near Paris in September 1938. It was meant to be an alternative to the Stalinist Comintern.
47225.m: The Fourth International was founded in 1938.

47226.q: Who murdered Trotsky in Mexico in 1940 on Stalin's orders?
47226.e: The Spanish agent struck Trotsky with an ice axe in Coyoacán. Trotsky died the next day.
47226.m: Trotsky was murdered by a Soviet agent in exile in Mexico in 1940.

47227.q: How did Trotsky describe the Soviet Union under Stalin in “The Revolution Betrayed”?
47227.e: Trotsky thought the property relations were still socialist, but a bureaucracy had seized power. Other left-wingers, by contrast, spoke of state capitalism.
47227.m: Trotsky saw Stalin's Soviet Union as a workers' state degenerated by bureaucracy.

47228.q: What was Leon Trotsky's real name?
47228.e: Trotsky was born in 1879 as Lev Davidovich Bronstein in what is now Ukraine. He took the name Trotsky after escaping from exile.
47228.m: Leon Trotsky's real name was Lev Bronstein.

47229.q: What is the tactic called in which Trotskyists join larger socialist parties as a group?
47229.e: In 1934 Trotsky advised his French followers to join the socialist party. There they were to win members for their ideas.
47229.m: In entryism, Trotskyists deliberately join larger parties.

47230.q: At which university did Rosa Luxemburg receive her doctorate in 1897?
47230.e: Women could already study in Zurich at that time. Her dissertation dealt with Poland's industrial development.
47230.m: Rosa Luxemburg completed her studies with a doctorate in Zurich.

47231.q: In which present-day country was Rosa Luxemburg born in 1871?
47231.e: She was born in Zamość, which then belonged to the Russian-ruled part of Poland. Later she gained German citizenship through a marriage of convenience.
47231.m: Rosa Luxemburg came from the then Russian part of Poland.

47232.q: What is Rosa Luxemburg's famous sentence about freedom?
a: “Freedom is always the freedom of those who think differently”
47232.e: The sentence appears as a note in the margin of her 1918 work “The Russian Revolution”. In it she criticised the Bolsheviks' suppression of the opposition.
47232.m: Rosa Luxemburg demanded freedom also for people with different opinions.

47233.q: With which work of 1899 did Rosa Luxemburg reply to Eduard Bernstein?
a: “The Mass Strike, the Political Party and the Trade Unions”
47233.e: Luxemburg held on to revolution and accused Bernstein of giving up socialism. Reforms alone, she said, could not overcome capitalism.
47233.m: Rosa Luxemburg defended the goal of revolution against Bernstein.

47234.q: What was the group around Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht that opposed the First World War called?
47234.e: The Spartacus League was named after the leader of a Roman slave revolt. It fought against the SPD's support for the war and became the seed of the KPD.
47234.m: Rosa Luxemburg led the Spartacus League with Karl Liebknecht.

47235.q: Why did Rosa Luxemburg oppose the First World War?
a: Because workers had to fight each other for the interests of the rulers
Because Germany had too few soldiers
Because she wanted to support Russia
Because she was against every form of politics
47235.e: For Rosa Luxemburg the war was an imperialist war. Workers of all countries should stick together instead of shooting at each other.
47235.m: Rosa Luxemburg saw the World War as a war against the workers.

47236.q: Which party did Rosa Luxemburg help to found around the turn of the year 1918/1919?
47236.e: The KPD grew out of the Spartacus League, which she led with Karl Liebknecht. The founding congress took place in Berlin.
47236.m: Rosa Luxemburg was a co-founder of the KPD.

47237.q: Who murdered Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht in Berlin in January 1919?
47237.e: After the Spartacist uprising, the two were abducted and murdered by officers of a Freikorps unit on 15 January 1919. The killers were hardly punished.
47237.m: Rosa Luxemburg was murdered by Freikorps soldiers in 1919.

47238.q: Which term is central for Antonio Gramsci to describe rule by consent rather than only by force?
47238.e: According to Gramsci, the ruling class secures its power mainly by having its values regarded as natural. Schools, churches and the press contribute to this.
47238.m: Gramsci explained rule through cultural hegemony.

47239.q: What are the notebooks that Gramsci wrote while held prisoner by the fascists called?
47239.e: In Italian they are called “Quaderni del carcere”. There are around 30 notebooks with notes on politics, culture and history.
47239.m: Gramsci's most important work is the Prison Notebooks.

47240.q: Which party did Antonio Gramsci help to found in 1921?
47240.e: At the Socialists' congress in Livorno in 1921, the left wing split off and founded the Communist Party of Italy. Gramsci later became its general secretary.
47240.m: In 1921 Gramsci was a co-founder of the Communist Party of Italy.

47241.q: What is the prosecutor in Gramsci's 1928 trial said to have demanded?
a: To stop this brain from working for twenty years
To deport Gramsci to the Soviet Union immediately
To read Gramsci's books out in public
47241.e: Gramsci was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison. Even so, he wrote down his most important ideas in prison.
47241.m: The fascists wanted to silence Gramsci through imprisonment.

47242.q: On which Italian island was Antonio Gramsci born in 1891?
47242.e: Gramsci was born in Ales and grew up in poor conditions. Later he studied in Turin with a scholarship.

47243.q: In which year did Antonio Gramsci die?
47243.e: He died in Rome in April 1937 as a result of his long imprisonment. His sentence had ended shortly before.
47243.m: Antonio Gramsci died in 1937 after years in prison.

47244.q: According to Gramsci, what role do intellectuals play for a social class?
a: They put its interests and world view into words
47244.e: Gramsci called such thinkers “organic intellectuals”. Every class produces its own thinkers, who give it awareness and cohesion.
47244.m: According to Gramsci, every class needs its own thinkers to express its view.

47245.q: Which military metaphor did Gramsci use for the long struggle for hegemony in Western societies?
47245.e: In Russia, a quick war of movement had been possible because civil society was weak. In the West, civil society had to be won step by step.
47245.m: Gramsci compared the struggle for hegemony in the West to a war of position.

47246.q: What did Eduard Bernstein demand of the SPD in the revisionism dispute?
a: The abolition of the trade unions
47246.e: Bernstein wanted to adapt Marxist theory to how things had actually developed. The SPD should openly see itself as a democratic reform party.
47246.m: Bernstein relied on reforms instead of revolution.

47247.q: How does Bernstein's famous sentence “The final goal, whatever it may be, is nothing to me, ...” end?
47247.e: For Bernstein, what counted were concrete improvements for the workers. He considered a distant final goal such as revolution to be secondary.
47247.m: For Bernstein, step-by-step progress mattered more than a distant final goal.

47248.q: In which Swiss city did Bernstein edit the newspaper “Der Sozialdemokrat” during Germany's Anti-Socialist Laws?
47248.e: The newspaper was printed in Switzerland and smuggled into Germany. In 1888 Bernstein was expelled and went to London.
47248.m: From Zurich, Bernstein produced a newspaper for the banned German Social Democrats.

47249.q: Which Marxist expectation did Bernstein reject?
47249.e: Bernstein observed that the middle class was not disappearing and crises were becoming milder. So he did not expect a collapse soon but relied on reforms.
47249.m: Bernstein did not believe capitalism would soon collapse.

47250.q: Which theorist, also called the “Pope of Marxism”, defended orthodox Marxism against Bernstein?
47250.e: Kautsky was editor of the journal “Die Neue Zeit”. He had also helped shape the SPD's Erfurt Programme.
47250.m: Karl Kautsky was regarded as the guardian of orthodox Marxism in the SPD.

47251.q: Which British reform movement influenced Bernstein during his time in London?
47251.e: The Fabians relied on gradual reforms instead of revolution. Bernstein lived in London until 1901 and came into contact with their ideas there.
47251.m: Bernstein's reformism was influenced by the British Fabians.

47252.q: With which programme did the SPD finally abandon Marxism as its foundation in 1959?
47252.e: After that the SPD saw itself as a people's party and accepted the market economy. In this way the reformist line won out in the long term.
47252.m: With the Godesberg Programme the SPD became a people's party.

47253.q: Who governed Russia immediately after the Tsar was overthrown in March 1917?
a: The Tsar's brother as the new Tsar
47253.e: The Provisional Government under Prince Georgy Lvov was to lead the country until a constituent assembly met. The Bolsheviks only took power in October 1917.
47253.m: After the Tsar's fall, a Provisional Government ruled first.

47254.q: What effect did “Order No. 1” of the Petrograd Soviet in March 1917 have on the Russian army?
a: The officers lost much of their authority over the soldiers
The army was placed under the Tsar again
47254.e: Order No. 1 allowed elected soldiers' committees and made government orders subject to the Soviet's approval. It badly undermined the officers' discipline.
47254.m: Order No. 1 weakened the officers' power over the soldiers.

47255.q: Which two centres of power faced each other in Russia after the February Revolution of 1917?
a: The Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet
47255.e: This is called dual power: the Provisional Government came from a committee of the Duma, while the Soviet represented workers and soldiers.
47255.m: After the February Revolution there was dual power in Russia.

47256.q: Why were there mass protests against the Provisional Government in April 1917?
a: It wanted to continue the war until victory
It wanted to bring back the Tsar
It had closed all the factories
47256.e: Foreign Minister Pavel Milyukov assured the Allies that Russia would fight on until victory. The April Crisis forced him to resign at the beginning of May 1917.
47256.m: Continuing the war cost the Provisional Government a lot of support.

47257.q: Which liberal party was most strongly represented in the first Provisional Government?
47257.e: The Constitutional Democrats, Kadets for short, provided several ministers in the first Provisional Government. They stood for a liberal, middle-class programme.
47257.m: The liberal Kadets shaped the first Provisional Government.

47258.q: Why did Tsar Nicholas II have to abdicate in March 1917?
a: The army leadership withdrew its support
The Bolsheviks had taken him prisoner
He had lost an election against the Duma
He wanted to retire to England
47258.e: As the unrest in Petrograd spread, his generals advised him to step down. Nicholas II signed the abdication in his train at Pskov.
47258.m: Without the support of his generals, Nicholas II had to abdicate in 1917.

47259.q: Which large industrial works in Petrograd locked out tens of thousands of workers in February 1917, fuelling the unrest?
47259.e: The Putilov Works were the largest arms factory in Petrograd. Locking out the workforce shortly before Women's Day drove many workers onto the streets.
47259.m: The lockout at the Putilov Works helped trigger the February Revolution.

47260.q: Which punishment did the Provisional Government abolish in March 1917 but reintroduce at the front in July 1917?
47260.e: The Provisional Government abolished the death penalty in March 1917. Because discipline was collapsing, it was reintroduced for soldiers at the front in July 1917.
47260.m: In 1917 the death penalty was first abolished and then reintroduced at the front.

47261.q: In which city on the Volga was Lenin born?
47261.e: Lenin was born in Simbirsk. Since 1924 the city has been called Ulyanovsk in his honour.
47261.m: Lenin's birthplace Simbirsk is now called Ulyanovsk.

47262.q: Which event of 1887 shaped the young Lenin and drove him towards revolution?
a: The execution of his elder brother
The assassination of Tsar Alexander II
The start of the First World War
47262.e: His brother Alexander Ulyanov was hanged in 1887 for a planned attempt on the Tsar's life. Tsar Alexander II had already been assassinated in 1881.
47262.m: The execution of his brother in 1887 radicalised Lenin.

47263.q: Which work by Lenin from 1902 called for a tightly organised party of professional revolutionaries?
47263.e: In “What Is to Be Done?” Lenin demanded a small, disciplined cadre party. “Das Kapital” and the “Manifesto” are by Marx and Engels, “The Revolution Betrayed” by Trotsky.
47263.m: Lenin's “What Is to Be Done?” set out the idea of the cadre party.

47264.q: Which woman was blamed for the assassination attempt in which Lenin was seriously injured in Moscow in August 1918?
47264.e: Lenin was shot on 30 August 1918 after a speech outside a Moscow factory. The Socialist Revolutionary Fanny Kaplan was arrested and shot a few days later.
47264.m: Fanny Kaplan was executed for the 1918 attempt on Lenin's life.

47265.q: In which country house near Moscow did Lenin die in January 1924?
47265.e: After several strokes, Lenin spent his last period in Gorki, south of Moscow. He died there on 21 January 1924.
47265.m: Lenin spent the last years of his life in Gorki near Moscow.

47266.q: Which decree did Lenin have the Congress of Soviets pass in November 1917 together with the Decree on Peace?
a: The Decree on the Gold Standard
The Decree on the Ban on Factions
47266.e: The Decree on Land took the large estates without compensation and gave the land to the peasants to use. It largely adopted the Socialist Revolutionaries' agricultural programme.
47266.m: Right after the October Revolution, Lenin's government shared out land to the peasants by decree.

47267.q: In which country did Lenin live in exile during the First World War until 1917?
47267.e: From 1914 Lenin lived in Bern and Zurich. In April 1917 he travelled to Russia in the sealed train with German permission.
47267.m: Lenin waited for the revolution in Zurich.

47268.q: Which ban did Lenin push through at the 10th Party Congress in March 1921?
a: The ban on factions within the party
47268.e: The resolution “On Party Unity” prohibited organised groups with their own platform. Later Stalin used this ban against his opponents.
47268.m: The 1921 ban on factions stifled open debate in the party.

47269.q: In which village in the Bernese Oberland did socialist opponents of the war meet for a second conference with Lenin in April 1916?
47269.e: After Zimmerwald in 1915, the Kiental Conference took place in April 1916. There Lenin tried to bring the opponents of the war onto a revolutionary course.
47269.m: The Kiental Conference of 1916 continued the meetings of war opponents in Switzerland.

47270.q: Why did the German government allow Lenin to travel through Germany to Russia in 1917?
a: It hoped Russia would be weakened and end the war
It wanted to arrest Lenin in Germany
It wanted Russia as an ally against Switzerland
It had been forced to do so by Switzerland
47270.e: Germany was fighting a war on two fronts. Lenin demanded an immediate end to the war, so the German leadership hoped he would take Russia out of the war.
47270.m: Germany helped Lenin in order to weaken Russia in the war.

47271.q: In which Swiss city did Lenin begin his journey in the sealed train in April 1917?
47271.e: Lenin's last home was on Spiegelgasse in Zurich. On 9 April 1917 he left Zurich main station with about 30 emigrants towards the German border.
47271.m: Lenin's journey to Russia began in Zurich in 1917.

47272.q: In which city did Lenin arrive at the end of his journey in April 1917 and give his first speech?
47272.e: On 16 April 1917 Lenin arrived at the Finland Station in Petrograd, today's St Petersburg. Shortly afterwards he presented his April Theses.
47272.m: In 1917 Lenin arrived at the Finland Station in Petrograd.

47273.q: Which Federal Councillor had to resign in June 1917 because he wanted to encourage a separate peace between Germany and Russia through a sounding-out attempt?
47273.e: In the Grimm-Hoffmann affair, a telegram from Federal Councillor Arthur Hoffmann to National Councillor Robert Grimm in Petrograd became public. The affair violated neutrality, and Hoffmann resigned.
47273.m: The Grimm-Hoffmann affair of 1917 led to a Federal Councillor's resignation.

47274.q: What did it mean that Lenin's carriage through Germany was “sealed”?
a: Nobody was allowed to get on or off on the way
The carriage was armoured against gunfire
The carriage ran without a locomotive
47274.e: The carriage counted as extraterritorial, like foreign territory. There were no checks, but also no contact with Germans during the journey.
47274.m: The sealed carriage was cut off from its surroundings.

47275.q: Through which neutral country did Lenin's group travel on to Russia after the journey through Germany?
47275.e: From the German Baltic coast they took the ferry to Sweden. Via Stockholm the group travelled north and then through Finland to Petrograd.
47275.m: In 1917 Lenin travelled to Russia via Sweden.

47276.q: What did the travellers promise in return for being allowed through?
a: To campaign for the release of Germans interned in Russia
To take Russia out of the Entente
47276.e: The emigrants promised to campaign in Russia for an exchange for Germans and Austrians interned there. In this way the journey looked like a prisoner exchange.
47276.m: In return, the travellers promised to support a prisoner exchange.

47277.q: Which force set off major fighting along the Trans-Siberian Railway with its revolt in May 1918?
47277.e: The legion of former prisoners of war was to be taken to France via Vladivostok. When the Bolsheviks tried to disarm it, it occupied large parts of the railway line.
47277.m: The revolt of the Czechoslovak Legion widened the civil war in 1918.

47278.q: Which White general advanced from the south as far as Oryol in 1919 and threatened Moscow?
47278.e: Denikin's Armed Forces of South Russia reached Oryol, about 350 kilometres south-west of Moscow, in October 1919. Then they were pushed back by the Red Army.
47278.m: Denikin's advance on Moscow failed at Oryol in 1919.

47279.q: To which city did the Bolsheviks move Russia's capital in March 1918?
47279.e: Petrograd was close to the front and in danger. So the government moved to Moscow, which has been the capital ever since.
47279.m: Since 1918 Moscow has again been Russia's capital.

47280.q: From which peninsula did General Wrangel evacuate his troops in November 1920?
47280.e: Wrangel held out in Crimea as the last White commander in the south. In November 1920 he took about 150,000 people by ship to Constantinople.
47280.m: The evacuation of Crimea in 1920 ended the Whites' fight in the south.

47281.q: Which anarchist led his own peasant army in Ukraine during the civil war?
47281.e: With his Revolutionary Insurgent Army, Nestor Makhno fought sometimes against the Whites, sometimes against the Reds. In 1921 he fled abroad.
47281.m: Nestor Makhno led an anarchist peasant movement in Ukraine.

47282.q: Which large peasant uprising of 1920 to 1921 was put down using poison gas, among other things?
47282.e: In Tambov province, peasants under Alexander Antonov rose up against the grain requisitions. The Red Army also used chemical weapons to crush them.
47282.m: The Tambov Rebellion showed the peasants' resistance to the Bolsheviks.

47283.q: What were the Bolsheviks' opponents in the Russian Civil War called?
47283.e: The Bolshevik “Reds” were opposed by the “Whites”. These included monarchists, officers and liberals, who often disagreed among themselves.
47283.m: In the Russian Civil War, Reds fought against Whites.

47284.q: Which city in the Far East did the Reds take in October 1922 as the last major stronghold of their opponents?
47284.e: Japanese troops withdrew from the Far East in 1922. On 25 October 1922 the Reds marched into Vladivostok.
47284.m: The capture of Vladivostok in 1922 ended the civil war in the Far East.

47285.q: What did peasants have to do under War Communism?
a: Hand over their grain to the state by force
Give their land back to the big landowners
Move to the factories in the cities
47285.e: Under this forced requisition, called prodrazvyorstka in Russian, the state decided how much grain each region had to hand over. Often even the seed grain was taken.
47285.m: Under War Communism, peasants had to hand over their grain to the state.

47486.q: What always came before the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig?
a: A prayer for peace in St Nicholas Church
A speech by the SED leadership
A football match in the stadium
47486.e: From the 1980s, prayers for peace were held every Monday in St Nicholas Church. Pastor Christian Führer opened the church with the motto “open to all”.
47486.m: The Monday demonstrations began after the prayers for peace in St Nicholas Church.

47487.q: What honorary name did Leipzig receive because of the Monday demonstrations?
47487.e: Since 1989 Leipzig has often been called the “City of Heroes” because peaceful protest there brought the breakthrough. The term “Trade Fair City”, on the other hand, refers to its old trading tradition.
47487.m: Because of the Monday demonstrations, Leipzig is also called the “City of Heroes”.

47488.q: Which citizens’ movement was founded in September 1989 and called for open dialogue in the GDR?
47488.e: New Forum published its appeal “Awakening 89” in September 1989. Many people at the Monday demonstrations supported its official recognition.
47488.m: New Forum was an important citizens’ movement in autumn 1989.

47489.q: What position did Günter Schabowski hold in November 1989?
a: Member of the Politburo and spokesman of the SED leadership
Chairman of the Council of Ministers
47489.e: Schabowski was a Politburo member and, as Central Committee secretary for information, was in charge of communication. That is why he informed the press about the decisions.
47489.m: In 1989 Günter Schabowski spoke for the SED leadership as a Politburo member.

47490.q: At the press conference on 9 November 1989, what did Schabowski answer when asked when the new travel rules would take effect?
47490.e: Schabowski leafed through his papers and said that, as far as he knew, the rules would take effect “immediately, without delay”. That same evening thousands of people streamed to the border crossings.
47490.m: Schabowski’s “immediately, without delay” led to the opening of the Wall.

47491.q: According to the GDR leadership’s plan, when were the new travel rules actually meant to take effect?
47491.e: The rules were embargoed and were only supposed to take effect on 10 November 1989, in an orderly way. Schabowski did not know about this embargo.
47491.m: The travel rules were actually only meant to apply from 10 November 1989.

47492.q: How did many GDR citizens find out about the opening of the border on the evening of 9 November 1989?
47492.e: On the news programme “Tagesthemen”, Hanns Joachim Friedrichs said: “The gates in the Wall are wide open.” Many GDR citizens watched West German television and then set off for the border.
47492.m: West German television carried the news of the open border into the GDR.

47493.q: What attitude did Günter Schabowski take towards the GDR after the fall of communism?
a: He openly criticised the GDR and his own role
He founded a new communist party
He emigrated to the Soviet Union
He became a minister in reunified Germany
47493.e: Schabowski was one of the few SED officials who looked critically at the GDR. He was convicted over the shootings at the Wall and died in Berlin in 2015.
47493.m: After 1989 Schabowski distanced himself from the GDR.

47494.q: What do the “Two” and the “Four” stand for in the name of the Two Plus Four Treaty?
a: West and East Germany plus the four victorious powers
West and East Germany plus four neighbouring countries
Two world wars and four occupation zones
Two alliances and four neutral states
47494.e: The two German states negotiated with the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France. Since 1945 these four powers had held rights concerning Germany as a whole.
47494.m: Two Plus Four: the two German states and the four victorious powers.

47495.q: Which weapons did reunified Germany renounce in the Two Plus Four Treaty?
47495.e: Germany confirmed that it would not make, own or control nuclear, biological or chemical weapons. Conventional weapons remained allowed.
47495.m: Reunified Germany renounced nuclear, biological and chemical weapons.

47496.q: What was the task of the Treuhandanstalt after the fall of communism?
a: To privatise or close the GDR’s state companies
To introduce the Deutschmark in the GDR
47496.e: The Treuhandanstalt was set up in 1990 and managed the GDR’s state-owned property. It sold companies, restructured them or closed them down.
47496.m: The Treuhand was meant to privatise the GDR economy.

47497.q: Roughly how many companies were under the Treuhandanstalt in summer 1990?
47497.e: On 1 July 1990 about 8,500 companies with around 45,000 sites were under the Treuhand. It was one of the largest business conglomerates in the world.

47498.q: Roughly how many people worked in the Treuhand companies at the start?
47498.e: At first the Treuhand companies employed around four million people. Many of them lost their jobs in the years that followed.
47498.m: At first about four million people worked in Treuhand companies.

47499.q: Which president of the Treuhandanstalt was murdered in April 1991?
47499.e: Detlev Karsten Rohwedder was shot dead in Düsseldorf on 1 April 1991; the Red Army Faction (RAF) claimed responsibility. The killers were never clearly identified.
47499.m: Treuhand president Rohwedder was murdered in 1991.

47500.q: Who ran the Treuhandanstalt from 1991 until it was wound up?
47500.e: Birgit Breuel, previously finance minister in Lower Saxony, took over in April 1991. She led the Treuhand until the end of 1994.
47500.m: Birgit Breuel ran the Treuhand until 1994.

47501.q: Why was the Treuhandanstalt unpopular with many people in eastern Germany?
a: Many companies were closed and jobs were lost
It banned travel to the West
47501.e: Hundreds of thousands lost their jobs when the Treuhand closed unprofitable companies. Many felt their economy was being sold off too cheaply to western firms.
47501.m: For many eastern Germans, the Treuhand is a symbol of unemployment after 1989.

47502.q: Which federal ministry is based today in the Detlev Rohwedder Building, the former Treuhand headquarters?
a: The Federal Ministry of the Interior
47502.e: The building on Leipziger Strasse was once the Reich Aviation Ministry and later the Treuhand headquarters. Since 1999 it has been used by the Federal Ministry of Finance.
47502.m: The Federal Ministry of Finance is based in the Detlev Rohwedder Building today.

47503.q: Which two words make up the German term “Ostalgie”?
47503.e: Ostalgie combines “Ost” (East) with “nostalgia”, a longing for the past. It means a rose-tinted memory of everyday life in the GDR.
47503.m: Ostalgie is a longing for everyday life in the GDR.

47504.q: Which 2003 film tells how a son pretends to his sick mother that the GDR still exists?
47504.e: In “Good Bye, Lenin!” by Wolfgang Becker, Alex recreates the GDR in the flat for his mother. The film is seen as an example of humorous Ostalgie.
47504.m: “Good Bye, Lenin!” shows the GDR with humour and wistfulness.

47505.q: What is the 1999 GDR comedy “Sonnenallee” about?
a: Everyday life of teenagers in East Berlin in the 1970s
An escape in a hot-air balloon
The Stasi spying on a writer
The building of the Berlin Wall in 1961
47505.e: The film by Leander Haussmann shows teenagers by the Wall with music, love and problems. It contributed a lot to the wave of Ostalgie.
47505.m: “Sonnenallee” shows growing up in East Berlin with humour.

47506.q: For which party did Walter Ulbricht sit in the Reichstag of the Weimar Republic from 1928?
47506.e: Ulbricht was an official of the Communist Party of Germany from early on and a member of the Reichstag from 1928 to 1933. After the Nazis came to power he went into exile.
47506.m: In the Weimar Republic, Walter Ulbricht was a KPD member of the Reichstag.

47507.q: Which committee of German émigrés and prisoners of war did Ulbricht help to found in the Soviet Union in 1943?
a: National Committee for a Free Germany
47507.e: The National Committee for a Free Germany used radio and leaflets to call on German soldiers to resist Hitler. Ulbricht was one of its communist founding members.
47507.m: In 1943 Ulbricht helped found the National Committee for a Free Germany.

47508.q: Which government office did Walter Ulbricht hold from the founding of the GDR in 1949?
47508.e: In 1949 Otto Grotewohl became Prime Minister and Wilhelm Pieck President. Ulbricht was Deputy Prime Minister, but through the party he held the real power.
47508.m: In 1949 Ulbricht was officially only Deputy Prime Minister.

47509.q: What did Ulbricht announce in July 1952 at the 2nd Party Conference of the SED?
47509.e: The construction of socialism brought forced collectivisation, pressure on small businesses and the churches, and heavy industry at the expense of consumer goods. The result was supply problems and a large wave of people fleeing.
47509.m: In 1952 Ulbricht proclaimed the planned construction of socialism.

47510.q: What rules of conduct for GDR citizens did Ulbricht set out at the 5th SED Party Congress in 1958?
a: Ten Commandments of Socialist Morality and Ethics
Seven Pillars of the Workers’ State
Five Laws of the Planned Economy
47510.e: The ten commandments were meant to replace the Christian commandments and demanded, for example, loyalty to the working class and love of the fatherland. They were added to the party programme in 1963.
47510.m: In 1958 Ulbricht announced the Ten Commandments of Socialist Morality.

47511.q: What did the so-called Ulbricht Doctrine of 1967 demand?
a: No Eastern Bloc relations with West Germany until it recognised the GDR
The withdrawal of all Soviet troops from the GDR
47511.e: The Ulbricht Doctrine was the answer to West Germany’s Hallstein Doctrine. Other Eastern Bloc states were only to establish diplomatic relations with Bonn once Bonn recognised the GDR.
47511.m: The Ulbricht Doctrine demanded that Bonn first recognise the GDR.

47512.q: Who was Prime Minister of the GDR in June 1953?
47512.e: Otto Grotewohl was Prime Minister, later Chairman of the Council of Ministers, from 1949 to 1964. He came from the SPD and was one of the two first chairmen of the SED.
47512.m: Otto Grotewohl led the GDR government in 1953.

47513.q: How was the uprising of 17 June 1953 crushed?
47513.e: The SED leadership could not end the uprising on its own. Soviet tanks rolled through East Berlin and other cities, and dozens of people died.

47514.q: Whose death in March 1953 led to a change of course in GDR policy?
47514.e: After Stalin’s death the new Soviet leadership pushed the SED to ease its harsh policies. But discontent among the population was already great.
47514.m: After Stalin’s death in 1953 the SED had to ease its course.

47515.q: What did the Soviet military administration impose on East Berlin and many districts on 17 June 1953?
a: An economic blockade of West Berlin
47515.e: Under the state of emergency, gatherings were banned and Soviet military courts judged demonstrators. In Berlin it lasted until July 1953.
47515.m: On 17 June 1953 the Soviets imposed a state of emergency.

47516.q: Apart from East Berlin, which industrial region was one of the centres of the 1953 uprising?
a: The area around Halle, Bitterfeld and Merseburg
The area around Rostock and Wismar
The area around Schwerin and Güstrow
The area around Görlitz and Zittau
47516.e: In the chemical triangle around Halle, Bitterfeld and Merseburg, especially many workers at large plants went on strike. In Bitterfeld strikers even formed a committee that briefly controlled the town.
47516.m: The chemical triangle around Halle was a centre of the 1953 uprising.

47517.q: Which Soviet party leader agreed to the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961?
47517.e: Without Moscow’s approval, the GDR could not have closed the border. Khrushchev gave the green light in early August 1961.
47517.m: Khrushchev allowed the building of the Wall in 1961.

47518.q: Who was Chancellor of West Germany when the Wall was built in 1961?
47518.e: Konrad Adenauer was Chancellor from 1949 to 1963. He was criticised because he only travelled to Berlin days after the Wall went up.
47518.m: When the Wall was built in 1961, Konrad Adenauer was Chancellor.

47519.q: Who was Governing Mayor of West Berlin in 1961?
47519.e: Willy Brandt was Governing Mayor from 1957 to 1966 and protested strongly against the sealing off of the border. He later became Chancellor.
47519.m: Willy Brandt governed West Berlin when the Wall was built.

47520.q: Who was the first person trying to escape to be shot dead in Berlin after the Wall was built?
47520.e: Günter Litfin was shot by transport police on 24 August 1961 while trying to swim across the Humboldt Harbour. Ida Siekmann had died two days earlier after jumping from a window.
47520.m: Günter Litfin was the first escapee shot dead at the Wall.

47521.q: What are the trials held after 1990 against border guards and their superiors called?
47521.e: In the Wall shooting trials, border guards and later also senior SED officials were convicted for the fatal shootings. The sentences for the soldiers were mostly lenient.
47521.m: After 1990 the Wall shooting trials dealt with the deaths at the border.

47522.q: How was the FDJ represented in the GDR’s People’s Chamber?
a: Not at all, it was banned
Only with an observer without a vote
Through a seat on the Council of State
47522.e: As a mass organisation, the FDJ received fixed seats through the National Front’s single list. In this way all parliamentary groups were under SED control from the start.
47522.m: The FDJ had its own parliamentary group in the People’s Chamber.

47523.q: Why did the FDJ hold a large torchlight procession in East Berlin on 6 October 1989?
a: For the 40th anniversary of the GDR
For the death of Walter Ulbricht
For the opening of the World Festival of Youth
For the 30th anniversary of the Wall
47523.e: Tens of thousands of FDJ members marched with torches in front of Honecker and the Soviet guest Gorbachev. Some of them shouted “Gorbi, help us!”.
47523.m: In 1989 the FDJ held a torchlight procession for the GDR’s 40th anniversary.

47524.q: Which large “Central Youth Project” of the FDJ was built in the Soviet Union from 1974?
a: A section of the Druzhba gas pipeline
47524.e: Thousands of young GDR workers built the gas pipeline that brought gas from the Soviet Union to Europe. The work was well paid and therefore sought after.
47524.m: From 1974 the FDJ helped build the gas pipeline in the Soviet Union.

47525.q: Which future SED General Secretary led the FDJ from 1974 to 1983?
47525.e: Egon Krenz rose to the top of the party through the youth organisation. The FDJ was seen as the SED’s training ground for officials.
47525.m: Egon Krenz was head of the FDJ from 1974 to 1983.

47526.q: What happened to the FDJ in West Germany in 1951?
a: It merged with the Young Union
47526.e: In 1951 the West German government banned the West German FDJ as an organisation hostile to the constitution. The ban was later upheld by the courts.
47526.m: In West Germany the FDJ was banned in 1951.

47527.q: Which FDJ singing group became known for the song “Sag mir, wo du stehst” (“Tell me where you stand”)?
47527.e: The Oktoberklub was formed in the 1960s as part of the FDJ singing movement. Puhdys, Karat and Silly, on the other hand, were rock bands.
47527.m: The Oktoberklub sang “Sag mir, wo du stehst”.

47528.q: Where did Hans-Dietrich Genscher announce on 30 September 1989 that thousands of GDR refugees could leave?
a: On the balcony of the West German embassy in Prague
In front of the Reichstag in Berlin
In St Nicholas Church in Leipzig
47528.e: Thousands of GDR citizens had fled into the grounds of the embassy in the Lobkowicz Palace. Genscher’s sentence was drowned out by the cheering crowd.
47528.m: In 1989 Genscher announced at the Prague embassy that the refugees could leave.

47529.q: Through which country did the special trains carrying the Prague embassy refugees have to travel in 1989?
47529.e: The GDR leadership insisted that the trains go through GDR territory so that the refugees could be formally stripped of citizenship. In Dresden many people therefore tried to jump on the trains.
47529.m: In 1989 the trains from Prague went through the GDR at the SED’s insistence.

47530.q: What were people called who helped GDR citizens escape, often for money?
47530.e: Escape helpers dug tunnels, forged passports or hid people in cars. In the GDR they were prosecuted as human traffickers and punished harshly.
47530.m: Escape helpers helped GDR citizens flee to the West.

47531.q: In which year did the GDR largely seal off the inner German border outside Berlin?
47531.e: From 1952 a restricted zone with a control strip was created along the inner German border. After that, Berlin remained the main loophole for escape until 1961.
47531.m: The inner German border was sealed off in 1952.

47532.q: What happened in 1952 to people in the GDR border area who were considered politically unreliable?
a: They were allowed to leave for the West
They were given new houses on the border
47532.e: In the so-called Operation Vermin, thousands of people were taken from their homes within hours. This was meant to secure the border area and make escape harder.
47532.m: In 1952 people from the GDR border area were forcibly resettled.

47533.q: Across which body of water did many GDR citizens try to reach the West by swimming or by boat?
47533.e: Destinations included the island of Fehmarn or Denmark. The Baltic was watched by border brigades, and many escapes ended in death or arrest.
47533.m: Many GDR citizens tried to escape across the Baltic Sea.

47534.q: Which chant of the demonstrators in Leipzig was aimed directly at the police and the workers’ militias?
47534.e: With “No violence!” people showed that they wanted to stay peaceful and asked the same of the security forces. This helped a great deal to ensure no blood was shed.
47534.m: “No violence!” was a key chant of the Leipzig demonstrations.

47535.q: Which altered chant at the Monday demonstrations showed the wish for reunification from late 1989?
47535.e: At first people chanted “We are the people!” and demanded a say in the GDR. After the fall of the Wall this became “We are one people!”, a demand for German unity.
47535.m: With “We are one people!” the demonstrators demanded unity.

47536.q: What is the “Runde Ecke” (Round Corner) in Leipzig today?
a: A museum in the former Stasi district headquarters
A concert hall of the Gewandhaus
47536.e: On 4 December 1989 citizens occupied the Stasi district headquarters at the “Runde Ecke”. Today a museum there shows the work of the secret police.
47536.m: Today the “Runde Ecke” houses a Stasi museum.

47537.q: With which annual festival does Leipzig remember the Peaceful Revolution on 9 October?
47537.e: Since 2009 thousands of people have gathered with candles on Augustusplatz on 9 October. The Festival of Lights recalls the great demonstration of 1989.
47537.m: Leipzig’s Festival of Lights remembers the Peaceful Revolution.

47538.q: Which newspaper did Günter Schabowski run as editor-in-chief from 1978 to 1985?
47538.e: “Neues Deutschland” was the SED’s central newspaper. As editor-in-chief, Schabowski was responsible for party propaganda.

47539.q: In which city did Schabowski lead the SED as its top official from 1985 to 1989?
47539.e: As First Secretary of the SED’s Berlin district leadership, Schabowski led the party in the GDR capital. At the same time he was a member of the Politburo.
47539.m: From 1985 Schabowski led the SED in East Berlin.

47540.q: Who gave Schabowski the note with the new travel rules shortly before the press conference?
47540.e: The new party leader handed Schabowski the paper without telling him clearly about the embargo. So Schabowski read the text out unprepared.
47540.m: Egon Krenz gave Schabowski the note with the travel rules.

47541.q: In which year was the Two Plus Four Treaty signed?
47541.e: The six foreign ministers signed the treaty in Moscow on 12 September 1990. A few weeks later, on 3 October 1990, Germany was reunified.
47541.m: The Two Plus Four Treaty was signed in 1990, shortly before reunification.

47542.q: Which border did the Two Plus Four Treaty fix as the final eastern border of reunified Germany?
47542.e: Reunified Germany only includes the territory of West Germany, the GDR and all of Berlin, and its borders are final. The border with Poland on the Oder and Neisse was also confirmed in November 1990 in the German-Polish Border Treaty.
47542.m: The Two Plus Four Treaty finally recognised the Oder-Neisse line.

47543.q: Which Soviet foreign minister negotiated the Two Plus Four Treaty?
47543.e: Eduard Shevardnadze was foreign minister under Gorbachev from 1985 to 1990. He later became President of Georgia.
47543.m: Eduard Shevardnadze represented the Soviet Union in the Two Plus Four talks.

47544.q: Unlike the Two Plus Four Treaty, which treaty dealt with the internal questions of German unity?
47544.e: The Unification Treaty between West and East Germany dealt with the GDR joining and with matters such as law and administration. The Two Plus Four Treaty settled the external questions with the victorious powers.
47544.m: The Unification Treaty settled the internal questions of unity, the Two Plus Four Treaty the external ones.

47545.q: What did the Two Plus Four Treaty settle for reunified Germany regarding alliances?
a: Germany may freely choose its alliances and stay in NATO
Germany must join the Warsaw Pact
47545.e: The treaty confirmed the right to belong to alliances. This meant reunified Germany could remain a member of NATO, which Gorbachev had already accepted.
47545.m: Under the treaty, reunified Germany was allowed to stay in NATO.

47546.q: Under the Two Plus Four Treaty, what may not be stationed on the territory of the former GDR?
47546.e: Foreign armed forces and nuclear weapons may not be stationed in eastern Germany. German army units, however, are allowed there.
47546.m: No foreign troops or nuclear weapons may be stationed in eastern Germany.

47547.q: What was the 1993 hunger strike by the miners of Bischofferode in Thuringia against?
a: The closure of their mine by the Treuhand
The opening of the Stasi files
47547.e: The miners protested for months against the closure of their potash mine. The hunger strike became a symbol of protest against Treuhand policy.
47547.m: In 1993 the Bischofferode hunger strike became a symbol of protest against the Treuhand.

47548.q: What mocking nickname did the Trabant have because of its body?
47548.e: The body was made of Duroplast, a plastic reinforced with cotton fibres. That is why people called the car, mockingly but fondly, “Rennpappe” (racing cardboard).
47548.m: The Trabant was popularly known as “Rennpappe” (racing cardboard).

47549.q: Which GDR products do many people in eastern Germany still buy today out of Ostalgie?
a: Spreewald gherkins and Rotkäppchen sparkling wine
47549.e: After 1990 many eastern products disappeared, but some came back and are very popular today. Spreewald gherkins and Rotkäppchen sparkling wine are well-known examples.
47549.m: Ostalgie also shows in the love of old GDR brands.

47550.q: Which non-religious celebration from GDR times do many teenagers in eastern Germany still celebrate today?
47550.e: The Jugendweihe marks the step into adult life at about 14. In the GDR it was almost compulsory, and it is still common in eastern Germany.
47550.m: The Jugendweihe is still celebrated in eastern Germany today.

47551.q: What do many historians criticise about Ostalgie?
a: That it plays down the dictatorship and the lack of freedom
That it is only common in western Germany
That it shows the planned economy too negatively
That it has not produced any products
47551.e: Ostalgie often recalls everyday life, community and products. Critics complain that the Stasi, the Wall and political persecution are left out.
47551.m: Critics accuse Ostalgie of playing down the GDR dictatorship.

47552.q: In which year was the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance founded?
47552.e: The Council was founded in Moscow in January 1949. It was meant to coordinate the economies of the Eastern Bloc states under Soviet leadership.
47552.m: The Council for Mutual Economic Assistance was founded in 1949 as the Eastern Bloc’s economic alliance.

47553.q: By what English abbreviation was the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance known in the West?
47553.e: Comecon stands for Council for Mutual Economic Assistance. It was the economic alliance of the Eastern Bloc.
47553.m: In the West the council was called Comecon.

47554.q: Which western programme was the founding of Comecon a response to?
47554.e: The Soviet Union banned its satellite states from taking part in the American Marshall Plan. Comecon was meant to link the economies of the Eastern Bloc instead.
47554.m: Comecon was the Eastern answer to the Marshall Plan.

47555.q: Which Southeast Asian country joined Comecon in 1978?
47555.e: Vietnam became a full member of Comecon in 1978. Laos and Cambodia had observer status at most.
47555.m: Vietnam was a member of Comecon from 1978.

47556.q: Why was trade between the Comecon states and the West difficult?
a: Eastern Bloc currencies were not freely convertible
The West bought no raw materials
The Comecon states had no ports
47556.e: GDR marks, roubles or złoty could not be freely exchanged for dollars. For western goods the states needed hard currency, which was always scarce.
47556.m: Non-convertible currencies made Eastern Bloc trade with the West difficult.

47557.q: Which socialist country worked with Comecon only as an associate member from 1964?
47557.e: After its break with Stalin, Yugoslavia was not part of the Eastern Bloc. From 1964, however, it took part in some areas of Comecon as an associate member.
47557.m: Yugoslavia was only an associate member of Comecon.

47558.q: In which city was the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance based?
47558.e: Comecon was founded in Moscow in 1949 and had its seat there. The Soviet Union was its economically strongest member.

47559.q: Which Hungarian manufacturer supplied buses to the whole Eastern Bloc as part of the division of labour in Comecon?
47559.e: In Comecon, countries were meant to specialise in certain products. With its Ikarus buses, Hungary became the largest bus producer in the Eastern Bloc.
47559.m: Ikarus buses from Hungary ran throughout the Eastern Bloc.

47560.q: Which of these countries was a founding member of Comecon in 1949?
47560.e: The founding members were the Soviet Union, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. The other states mentioned only joined later.
47560.m: Romania belonged to Comecon from the start.

47561.q: On what day was martial law declared in Poland?
47561.e: During the night of 13 December 1981 the Polish leadership imposed martial law. Tanks appeared on the streets and thousands of opposition members were interned.
47561.m: Martial law in Poland began on 13 December 1981.

47562.q: What did US President Ronald Reagan call on people to do at Christmas 1981 as a sign of solidarity with Poland?
a: Put a candle in the window
47562.e: Reagan asked people in the USA to put a candle in their window as a sign of support for the Polish people. At the same time the USA imposed sanctions on Poland.
47562.m: In 1981 candles in windows showed the West’s solidarity with Poland.

47563.q: What was the body that held power in Poland during martial law called?
47563.e: The Military Council of National Salvation (WRON in Polish) under Jaruzelski governed during martial law. It was made up of senior officers.
47563.m: During martial law Poland was ruled by a military council.

47564.q: Which organisation was martial law in Poland mainly meant to suppress?
47564.e: The independent trade union Solidarność had about ten million members. Under martial law it was suspended and in 1982 officially banned.
47564.m: Martial law was aimed mainly at Solidarność.

47565.q: At which coal mine were nine striking miners shot dead in December 1981?
47565.e: On 16 December 1981 special militia units fired on striking miners at the Wujek mine. Nine people died; it was the bloodiest incident of martial law.
47565.m: Nine striking miners died at the Wujek mine in 1981.

47566.q: In which year was martial law in Poland officially lifted?
47566.e: Martial law was suspended at the end of 1982 and formally lifted on 22 July 1983. Many restrictions, however, stayed in place in laws.
47566.m: Martial law in Poland officially ended in July 1983.

47567.q: What happened to Lech Wałęsa after martial law was imposed?
a: He was interned for about eleven months
47567.e: Wałęsa was arrested on the night of 13 December 1981 and interned until 14 November 1982. After that he remained under state security surveillance.
47567.m: Lech Wałęsa was interned for almost a year during martial law.

47568.q: What was Jaruzelski’s main justification for martial law later on?
a: It had prevented a Soviet invasion
It had ended a civil war in the GDR
It had prevented a famine in Hungary
47568.e: Jaruzelski called martial law the “lesser evil” that had prevented a Soviet invasion. Whether this danger really existed is disputed among historians.
47568.m: Jaruzelski called martial law a lesser evil compared with a Soviet invasion.

47569.q: What was Lech Wałęsa’s job at the Gdańsk shipyard?
47569.e: Lech Wałęsa worked as an electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk. He was sacked in 1976 because of his activism.
47569.m: Lech Wałęsa was a trained electrician.

47570.q: What triggered the strike at the Gdańsk shipyard in August 1980?
a: The sacking of a crane operator shortly before retirement
The planned closure of the shipyard
47570.e: The popular crane operator Anna Walentynowicz was sacked shortly before her retirement. The strike first demanded her reinstatement and then quickly spread.
47570.m: The sacking of a crane operator was the spark for the Gdańsk strike.

47571.q: Which office did Lech Wałęsa hold from 1990 to 1995?
47571.e: Wałęsa won Poland’s first free presidential election in 1990. Five years later he narrowly lost his bid for re-election.
47571.m: Lech Wałęsa was President of Poland from 1990 to 1995.

47572.q: Who accepted the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo in 1983 on behalf of Lech Wałęsa?
47572.e: Wałęsa feared he would not be allowed back into Poland if he left. So his wife Danuta accepted the prize.
47572.m: Danuta Wałęsa accepted the Nobel Peace Prize for her husband.

47573.q: According to his own account, how did Lech Wałęsa get into the shipyard on strike in Gdańsk in August 1980?
a: He climbed over the shipyard wall
He was hidden in a lorry
47573.e: Wałęsa had been sacked in 1976 and was not allowed onto the shipyard. According to his own account, he climbed over the shipyard wall on 14 August 1980 and took charge of the strike.
47573.m: In 1980 Wałęsa climbed over the shipyard wall to lead the strike.

47574.q: Who beat Lech Wałęsa in the 1995 presidential election?
47574.e: The post-communist Aleksander Kwaśniewski narrowly won the 1995 run-off against Wałęsa and became his successor.
47574.m: In 1995 Wałęsa lost to the post-communist Kwaśniewski.

47575.q: What is the agreement of 31 August 1980 called, in which the government allowed free trade unions?
47575.e: In the Gdańsk Agreement the government recognised the right to strike and independent trade unions. Wałęsa signed it with a strikingly large ballpoint pen.
47575.m: The 1980 Gdańsk Agreement made the founding of Solidarność possible.

47576.q: How many demands did the Gdańsk strike committee draw up in 1980?
47576.e: The 21 demands were put up on wooden boards at the shipyard gate. First on the list was permission for free trade unions.

47577.q: Which airport is named after Lech Wałęsa?
47577.e: Since 2004 Gdańsk airport has been called Gdańsk Lech Wałęsa Airport. Warsaw airport is named after Frédéric Chopin.
47577.m: Gdańsk airport is named after Lech Wałęsa.

47578.q: During which period did the Round Table meet in Poland?
47578.e: The talks between the government and the opposition began in Warsaw on 6 February and ended on 5 April 1989.
47578.m: The Polish Round Table met in spring 1989.

47579.q: Under the Round Table agreements, what share of the seats in the Sejm was freely elected in 1989?
47579.e: 65 per cent of the Sejm seats were reserved for the communist PZPR and its allies. Only 35 per cent could be freely contested.
47579.m: In the 1989 Sejm election only just over a third of the seats were freely elected.

47580.q: Which chamber of parliament was brought back by the Round Table agreements and elected completely freely?
47580.e: The Senate with 100 seats was newly created. Its members were chosen in a free election without quotas in 1989.
47580.m: In 1989 the Polish Senate was brought back as a freely elected chamber.

47581.q: How many of the 100 Senate seats did Solidarność win in the 1989 election?
47581.e: Solidarność won 99 of the 100 Senate seats; the last went to an independent candidate. It also won all 161 freely contested seats in the Sejm.
47581.m: In 1989 Solidarność won almost all the seats in the Senate.

47582.q: On what date was the first round of the partly free parliamentary election held in Poland?
47582.e: Poland voted on 4 June 1989. On the same day the Chinese government crushed the protests in Tiananmen Square.
47582.m: On 4 June 1989 Poland held its first partly free election.

47583.q: Who became the first non-communist head of government in the Eastern Bloc in 1989?
47583.e: The Catholic journalist Tadeusz Mazowiecki was elected Prime Minister by the Sejm in August 1989.
47583.m: In 1989 Tadeusz Mazowiecki led the first non-communist government in the Eastern Bloc.

47584.q: Who negotiated with each other at the Round Table in Poland in 1989?
a: The communist government and the opposition around Solidarność
The trade unions and the employers
47584.e: At the Round Table sat representatives of the government around Interior Minister Kiszczak and of the opposition around Lech Wałęsa. The Church mediated between them.
47584.m: At the Round Table the government and the opposition negotiated.

47585.q: What did Solidarność itself achieve at the Round Table?
47585.e: In April 1989 Solidarność was officially allowed again. This meant it could take part in the June election as a citizens’ committee.
47585.m: Thanks to the Round Table, Solidarność was allowed again in 1989.

47586.q: The 1976 trial of which rock band was an important reason for Charter 77?
a: The Plastic People of the Universe
47586.e: The conviction of the musicians of the underground band The Plastic People of the Universe outraged intellectuals. This led to the idea of a joint declaration.
47586.m: The trial of the Plastic People sparked Charter 77.

47587.q: Which international document did Charter 77 mainly refer to?
a: The 1945 Charter of the United Nations
47587.e: In 1975 Czechoslovakia had signed the CSCE Final Act and ratified human rights covenants. Charter 77 demanded that the state keep these promises.
47587.m: Charter 77 demanded that the Helsinki Final Act be respected.

47588.q: Which writer was one of the first spokespeople of Charter 77 and became President of Czechoslovakia in 1989?
47588.e: Václav Havel was imprisoned several times for his activism. After the Velvet Revolution, parliament elected him President in December 1989.
47588.m: Václav Havel went from Charter 77 to the presidency.

47589.q: Roughly how many people signed Charter 77 when it was published in January 1977?
47589.e: At first the declaration had about 240 signatures. By 1989 almost 2,000 people had signed it in total.
47589.m: Charter 77 began with about 240 brave signatories.

47590.q: What was the counter-declaration to Charter 77 called, organised by the regime and signed by many artists under pressure?
47590.e: In January 1977 well-known artists had to sign a declaration against Charter 77 at the National Theatre. It became known as the “Anti-Charter”.
47590.m: The regime used the Anti-Charter to fight Charter 77.

47591.q: What was Václav Havel known as before his political career?
47591.e: Havel wrote absurdist plays such as “The Garden Party” and “Audience”. Because he criticised the regime, for a long time they could only be performed abroad.
47591.m: Václav Havel was a well-known Czech playwright.

47592.q: What is the title of Václav Havel’s famous 1978 essay about life under late communism?
47592.e: In this essay Havel describes a greengrocer who puts slogans in his shop window. He calls on people to “live in truth”.
47592.m: Havel’s essay “The Power of the Powerless” called for living in truth.

47593.q: Which committee did Václav Havel help to found in 1978?
a: Committee for the Defence of the Unjustly Prosecuted
47593.e: The committee (VONS in Czech) documented cases of political persecution. Because of this, Havel was sentenced in 1979 to several years in prison.
47593.m: In VONS Havel stood up for people persecuted for political reasons.

47594.q: Which office did Václav Havel hold from 1993 to 2003?
a: First President of the Czech Republic
47594.e: After Czechoslovakia split, Havel became the first President of the Czech Republic in 1993. He served two terms until 2003.
47594.m: Havel was the first President of the Czech Republic.

47595.q: Which President of Czechoslovakia resigned in December 1989?
47595.e: Gustáv Husák had been President since 1975. On 10 December 1989 he swore in the new government and then resigned.
47595.m: Husák’s resignation in 1989 ended the era of “normalisation”.

47596.q: Which 1939 event did the student demonstration that started the Velvet Revolution commemorate?
a: The closure of Czech universities by the Nazis
The invasion by the Red Army
47596.e: In November 1939 the German occupiers closed the Czech universities after the student Jan Opletal died. The anniversary was officially allowed.
47596.m: The demonstration on 17 November 1989 commemorated the repression of students in 1939.

47597.q: Who became President of Czechoslovakia in December 1989?
47597.e: The writer Václav Havel was spokesman of the Civic Forum and had been in prison as a critic of the regime. On 29 December 1989 parliament elected him President.
47597.m: Václav Havel became President of Czechoslovakia in 1989.

47598.q: What was the Slovak partner movement of the Civic Forum called?
47598.e: The movement “Public Against Violence” (VPN) was founded in Bratislava. It worked closely with the Civic Forum in Prague.
47598.m: In Slovakia the Public Against Violence movement led the protests.

47599.q: Which symbolic gesture by the demonstrators in Wenceslas Square became especially famous?
47599.e: People jingled their keys. This was meant to tell the communist leaders that their time was up and they should go.
47599.m: Jingling keys became a symbol of the Velvet Revolution.

47600.q: How long did the nationwide general strike of 27 November 1989 in Czechoslovakia last?
47600.e: On 27 November 1989 millions of people stopped work from 12 noon to 2 pm. The short strike showed the broad support for the opposition.
47600.m: In 1989 a two-hour general strike showed the strength of the opposition.

47601.q: What is the peaceful split of Czechoslovakia on 1 January 1993 called?
47601.e: In reference to the Velvet Revolution it is called the Velvet Divorce. The Czech Republic and Slovakia separated without a referendum and without violence.
47601.m: In 1993 Czechoslovakia split peacefully into two states.

47602.q: What did the Czechoslovak parliament remove from the constitution on 29 November 1989?
a: The leading role of the Communist Party
47602.e: Under pressure from the protests, the article on the leading role of the KSČ was deleted. This ended the party’s monopoly on power.
47602.m: At the end of November 1989 the KSČ lost its leading role guaranteed in the constitution.

47603.q: Which politician and his Pan-European Union were behind the Pan-European Picnic?
47603.e: Otto von Habsburg, son of the last Austrian emperor, was President of the Pan-European Union. He organised the picnic with Hungarian opposition members.
47603.m: Otto von Habsburg was patron of the Pan-European Picnic.

47604.q: Near which Hungarian town did the Pan-European Picnic take place?
47604.e: The picnic took place near Sopron, Ödenburg in German, close to the border with Austria. The town lies in the far west of Hungary.
47604.m: The Pan-European Picnic took place near Sopron.

47605.q: Who used the Pan-European Picnic on 19 August 1989 to escape to the West?
47605.e: Many GDR citizens were on holiday in Hungary hoping for a chance to escape. At the picnic about 600 of them fled through the opened border gate into Austria.
47605.m: Hundreds of GDR citizens escaped at the Pan-European Picnic.

47606.q: What happened at the Pan-European Picnic on the Hungarian-Austrian border?
a: A border gate was opened for a short time
47606.e: As a symbolic gesture, a border gate was to be open for three hours. GDR citizens used the opportunity for a mass escape.
47606.m: At the Pan-European Picnic a border gate opened briefly.

47607.q: Which country did those fleeing at the Pan-European Picnic reach first?
47607.e: The border gate lay between Hungary and the Austrian state of Burgenland. From Austria the refugees travelled on to West Germany.
47607.m: In 1989 the refugees reached Austria first.

47608.q: What did the foreign ministers of Austria and Hungary do in front of the cameras in June 1989?
a: They cut through the border fence
47608.e: On 27 June 1989 Alois Mock and Gyula Horn cut the barbed wire near Sopron. The pictures went round the world and encouraged many GDR citizens to flee via Hungary.
47608.m: In 1989 two foreign ministers symbolically cut through the Iron Curtain.

47609.q: Why did the mass escape at the Pan-European Picnic happen without bloodshed?
a: The Hungarian border guards did not intervene
The border had already been completely dismantled
47609.e: The officer in charge had no clear orders and decided not to have anyone shoot. So hundreds of people could walk peacefully across the border.
47609.m: In 1989 Hungarian border guards let the refugees go.

47610.q: What was the significance of the Pan-European Picnic for the end of the GDR?
a: It showed that the Iron Curtain was becoming porous
It led directly to Helmut Kohl’s election
It ended the Warsaw Pact immediately
It triggered the building of a new wall
47610.e: The mass escape showed that the Soviet Union was no longer stepping in. After that, more and more GDR citizens fled via Hungary, which greatly increased the pressure on the SED.
47610.m: The Pan-European Picnic made the Iron Curtain porous.

47611.q: What had Hungary already started doing in May 1989?
a: Taking down the border fence with Austria
47611.e: On 2 May 1989 Hungary began to take down the electric alarm systems and the barbed wire on the border with Austria. One official reason was also the high maintenance costs.
47611.m: In May 1989 Hungary became the first Eastern Bloc country to start taking down its border fence.

47612.q: How did Nicolae Ceaușescu’s life end in December 1989?
a: He was executed after a rushed trial
He fled into exile in Moscow
He resigned and lived in Bucharest
He was sentenced to life imprisonment
47612.e: Ceaușescu and his wife Elena fled Bucharest but were caught. A military court sentenced them to death in a short trial, and the sentence was carried out at once.
47612.m: In 1989 Ceaușescu was executed after a rushed trial.

47613.q: The threatened eviction of which pastor sparked the protests in Timișoara?
47613.e: The Hungarian Reformed pastor László Tőkés openly criticised the regime. Members of his congregation protected his flat, and this grew into a popular uprising.
47613.m: The resistance around Pastor László Tőkés started the Romanian Revolution.

47614.q: Which building did rebels occupy on 22 December 1989, so that the revolution was broadcast live?
47614.e: Revolutionaries occupied the state television building in Bucharest. The events were broadcast live, so people spoke of a televised revolution.
47614.m: The Romanian Revolution was broadcast live on television.

47615.q: On what day were Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu executed?
47615.e: After a short trial before a military court, the couple were shot on Christmas Day 1989.
47615.m: The Ceaușescus were executed on Christmas Day 1989.

47616.q: Which group took power in Romania after Ceaușescu’s fall?
47616.e: The National Salvation Front was made up mainly of former communists and officers. It formed the interim government.
47616.m: After Ceaușescu, the National Salvation Front governed.
